📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar reveals how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

Recent findings suggest that in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

Recent findings suggest that in the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that meta has turned down the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority over testing its Muse agent, WIRED reported on Thursday. The regulator had suggested testing Muse jointly in its sandbox. Colin Payne, the FCA’s head of innovation, said the offer came last week, Isabella Ward reported for WIRED.

Meta only told the FCA about Muse last month, according to WIRED. The agent arrived in the UK on Tuesday.

“If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” Payne stated, according to WIRED.

Payne also warned that more agents are on their way.

“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” he mentioned, WIRED reported.

The FCA set out its expectations for AI agent builders on Tuesday, the day Muse released. Its agentic AI page says the FCA’s AI Lab offers services to help firms develop and test newly introduced agentic products.

“We have powers to intervene if we believe regulated financial services are being offered without our authorisation,” the FCA says on the page.

Sources indicate that the FCA is not the only regulator watching. Other UK watchdogs, including the competition and data regulators, have warned Meta about consumer protection law, WIRED reported.

Meta noted it has been talking to regulators.

“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta spokesperson Matthew Pollard stated in a statement to WIRED.

#132298. The history of civilization is the history of wheat

The history of civilization is the history of wheat

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Asteriskmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving.
  • In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides.
  • The ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that according to Sumerian myth, when the world was young, there was no farming, no cattle, and no weaving. The original gods were forced to live in poverty. To solve this problem they created Ashnan, the goddess of grain, and Lahar, the god of sheep, and sent them to humans to cultivate their gifts.

In a recent development, together, Ashnan and Lahar furnished the rest of the pantheon with bread, beer, milk, and hides. But the fresh gods quarreled about which was greater. Enki, the god of wisdom, judged Ashnan the superior, reasoning that without grain there would be no bread, no beer, and, by extension, no cities and no Sumer.

The ancient Sumerians recognized something still true today: The story of wheat is the story of people. Human consumption of wheat is older than cities, older than writing, older than the wheel. In fact, some of the very earliest surviving examples of writing, which, like wheat, originate in the Middle East, aren’t epic poems or religious texts but administrative records of the storage and taxation of grain. Other staple crops dominated in other parts of the world (like rice in East Asia, and maize in the Americas), but it was wheat that fueled the Roman Empire and the Industrial Revolution. Wheat now provides one-fifth of the world’s calories. The fact that it does so is thanks to centuries of human ingenuity and scientific improvement.

Six thousand years ago, when the Sumerian civilization was beginning to emerge in what is now Iraq, human consumption of grain was already ancient history. Remains of domesticated wheat from around 10,000 years ago have been found in Anatolia. These leftovers were wild emmer and einkorn (two progenitors of wheat), which looked a lot like the other wild grasses growing around them: a tall stalk topped by a small seed head. They were variably distributed throughout the landscape, and their seeds ripened at different times, so collecting them would have been laborious. Nonetheless, the people of the ancient Levant found the effort worthwhile, as the seeds were calorie-dense and stored well.

By farming wheat, humans unintentionally made it worse but also improved it. Wild wheat had reproduced without human assistance for millions of years. Its seeds, the grains that we eat, are attached to the head of the plant by a thin stalk called a rachis. When the seeds are mature, the rachis shatters, dispersing the seeds on the ground.

Industry observers note that this process is essential for wild wheat to reproduce. Human intervention removed this selection pressure, allowing plants that did not shatter to reproduce. Because nonshattering is a recessive trait, nonshattering plants cannot produce shattering offspring.1 As a result, nonshattering plants proliferated, supplanting their wild predecessors. This is how archaeologists observed that domestication was underway.2.

Neolithic farmers collected and planted seeds from the heads of plants that remained intact, whereas seeds that had already fallen to the ground were less likely to be harvested or planted. Stores of emmer and einkorn dated as early as 7600 B.C.E. show rough scars, not the smooth tears left by spontaneous shattering, indicating that the natural reproductive process had been interrupted by harvesters. Once the seed-shattering trait had disappeared, wheat was almost completely dependent on humans collecting and planting its seeds to reproduce. In perhaps a thousand years, millions of years of selection for seed shattering had been undone.

On the positive side, yields went up. Grains grew bigger thanks to human cultivation. Naturally, grain size varied, but larger grains were less likely to be blown away or slip out of harvesters’ baskets and were therefore overrepresented in the seeds saved and replanted. On top of that, humans tend to plant seeds deeper than they naturally scatter, and larger seeds are more likely to germinate at greater depths. These processes are thought to have increased grain size by a quarter over the first 500 to 1,000 years of cultivation. By this time, wheat could no longer thrive without help from humans. But the transition to agrarian, sedentary communities enabled by bigger harvests also marked the beginning of our dependence on farming.

The next crucial step came just as wheat was beginning to spread to surrounding regions, when it absorbed a whole latest set of genes from another species.

It has been revealed that one way plants differ from animals is that they can hybridize much more easily, sometimes even happily adding whole fresh genomes to their own. Long before domestication, emmer wheat had already done this: Wild emmer is a naturally occurring amalgam of a cousin of einkorn and another species known as goat grass (Aegilops speltoides). Emmer is therefore tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.

In a recent development, emmer and einkorn wheat diffused throughout Anatolia to Cyprus and beyond as farmers migrated out of the Fertile Crescent. Around this time, emmer hybridized again, incorporating the genome of a second species of goat grass (Aegilops tauschii), bringing its chromosome set count to six. This hybridized wheat, which first appears in the archaeological record in northeastern Turkey around 6000 B.C.E., thrived because it had two valuable traits. First, it was free-threshing. Before this, farmers had to pound grains with a mortar and pestle to free them from their tough outer husks, adding a labor-intensive step to every harvest. Second, this upcoming hybrid had higher gluten content, meaning it could form stronger doughs that hold gas, allowing bread to rise. Initially, this saved labor and enabled tastier food. It is now known as bread wheat, or common wheat, and makes up more than 95% of wheat produced today.

Over the next several millennia, cultivation of bread wheat (and agriculture, more or less) spread throughout Europe and Asia. If a plant failed to grow in its upcoming soil or was killed by autumn frosts before reaching maturity, it would be superseded by its better-acclimated relatives. Over thousands of years, incremental changes resulted in countless subtly different local “landrace” populations. Wheat also evolved through further hybridization with closely related plants. This is how we got spelt, which combined the larger grains of bread wheat with the strong shells of emmer, protecting it against the wet and cold and allowing it to thrive further north.

Sources indicate that much of this adaptation was probably incidental, just as early selection for larger seeds and nonbrittle rachises had been. But even in ancient times, careful attention was paid to wheat husbandry and to which varieties thrived in which environments. In 50 B.C.E., the Roman writer Varro advised farmers that “on the threshing-floor the largest and best ears should be placed apart, to furnish the best seed.”3 Long before genetics, farmers understood that good seed begat good crops. This contributed to thousands of years of gradual improvement and specialization.

Industry observers note that the Romans may have been intentionally selecting the best plants, but modern scientific wheat breeding began in western Europe in the 19th century. This dramatically sped up yield improvements. A fortuitously large number of early English estate records have survived, meaning we have data for wheat yields starting from before 1275, at which time farmers were producing around 0.6 metric tons per hectare. This was actually worse than the (continental) Romans, who achieved yields up to 1.3 metric tons per hectare.4 Yields remained approximately flat before the 16th century, when they began increasing (and have not stopped).

From the early 1600s through to 1805, yields in Britain almost doubled, increasing from 0.74 in 1604 to 1.26 metric tons per hectare in 1805.5 Deliberate plant selection contributed to this improvement, but intensive selection — that is, aggressively multiplying the very best strains — didn’t really take off until the second half of the 18th century.

According to recent reports, farmers had always wanted to find high-performing seeds, but now they could buy them. Seedsmen emerged, trading hyperadapted local variants like Red Lammas, a strain popular in the 18th century that was known for thriving in chalky soils and making good-quality flour.

Cereals were big business: The original London Corn Exchange6 was built in 1747; the Paris exchange in 1767; Amsterdam had its own Korenbeurs more than a century earlier. From 1765, Britons began importing wheat with the express purpose of finding better varieties, and middlemen living in other countries would send samples of promising grains to contacts in Britain. Yields reflect the results of an increasingly commercialized sector. After stasis for hundreds of years, then steady 2.5% per decade growth in the previous two centuries, yields grew 60% between 1805 and 1865.

It has been revealed that in the 19th century, progress was still driven by entrepreneurs, usually curious farmers, rather than scientists. One key innovation, pioneered by Patrick Shirreff in Scotland and John Le Couteur in Jersey, was transitioning from selecting a handful of the best plants to breed from, to selecting the best single individual plant, and multiplying it. They didn’t understand the underlying biology, but the results were clear.

In addition to producing more of the best strains, repeated selection and rebreeding of individuals made the traits of the multiplied strains more consistent from generation to generation. As with shattering seed heads 10,000 years earlier, rebreeding meant undesirable genetic variants were eliminated from the population. Early breeders called this “breeding true,” and though the genetic basis for it was not yet understood, it was important to farmers, who prefer more consistent and predictable crops.

In a recent development, another key development was the intentional crossing of two plants to create a hybrid. A wheat plant can self-pollinate because it contains both male and female reproductive organs, fertilizing its ovules with its own pollen. The overwhelming majority of wheat plants are produced in this way, and therefore have just one parent, which acts genetically as both mother and father. This process doesn’t produce clones initially because each pollen grain or ovule, even from the same individual, is genetically distinct. But it does result in offspring with extremely limited genetic diversity, which diminishes even further with each successive generation of self-breeding.7.

Sources indicate that but sometimes cross-pollination produces plants that come from two parents rather than one. In nature this occurs randomly, but plant breeders deliberately take pollen from one plant and use it to fertilize the ovule of another. Shirreff was a pioneer of this technique, too. The best offspring resulting from these crosses would outperform both parents on some key traits. These high-performing varieties would then be multiplied and the seed sold to farmers.

Recent findings suggest that these techniques were adopted throughout Europe, where the Vilmorin Seed Manufacturer in France and the Swedish Seed Association in Sweden were among the first to institutionalize cereal breeding. In 1884, The Technology of Bread-Making identified as many as 65 wheat varieties, local and imported, available in English grain markets.

In a recent development, before the Industrial Revolution, Britain was a largely agricultural nation. But by the end of the 19th century, the population had increased more than sevenfold from about 4 million people in 1600 to 30 million in 1900, and only a tenth of workers were employed in agriculture. This would have been impossible without improvements in agricultural yields. The “dark satanic mills” of the Industrial Revolution needed wheat just as much as they needed coal and child labor.

The pace of improvement increased as researchers began to understand more about genetics and evolution. The discoveries of Darwin (natural selection) and Mendel (the inheritance of simple genetic traits, like seed shattering) were essential to understanding why and how techniques applied over the previous centuries had worked. Also critical were contributions of Wilhelm Johannsen, who untangled how much traits were shaped by genes as opposed to the environment, and Ronald Fisher, the “father of modern statistics,” who figured out the underlying maths. Fisher also highlighted how continuous traits like height could be determined by the cumulative effect of many individual genes. These insights, around 100 years ago, led to the development and widespread adoption of statistical tools to identify the best seed varieties and to predict how their offspring would perform.

Breeders generated a vast array of upcoming varieties for testing through a combination of exploration and crossing. Exploration, which was often sponsored by the state, meant collecting seeds from the many unique wheat varieties that had proliferated across the earth since the dawn of time. Britain’s Watkins Landrace Wheat Collection, for example, created in the 1930s, acquired more than 800 wheat cultivars from 32 countries, which could be crossed to create more than 300,000 new hybrid varieties. The USDA had the largest program. Using genetic material from these collections, nurseries would generate crosses for initial testing, multiplying the seeds until there were enough to carry out trials. Trials across several locations allowed researchers to distinguish the effects of genes and environment.

Recent findings suggest that but there were still constraints holding back wheat yields. One was wheat rust, a fungal disease that leaves a characteristic orange-brown powdery residue on plants before shriveling and killing them. Ancient writers knew about this disease: The Romans even had a yearly festival, the Robigalia, in which they performed rituals meant to keep it at bay. In the worst-affected years of the mid-20th century, wheat rust was killing off nearly 20% of American wheat. Breeding programs developed resistant varieties, but any respite was short-lived as the fungus would quickly evolve a newly introduced line of attack.

Another was wheat plants “lodging,” or falling over under their own weight. Fertilizer had become much cheaper thanks to the Haber-Bosch process for making ammonia from nitrogen gas, developed in 1909. But its usefulness for improving wheat production was limited because although fertilizer could in theory make the plants grow larger than before, applying it would often make the stems collapse, making the wheat unharvestable.

According to recent reports, at the time, these problems seemed to show that there were fundamental trade-offs limiting yields. It was assumed that further improvements would be incremental. This fueled worry that there would soon be insufficient food for the growing global population; biologist Paul Ehrlich predicted in 1968 that “in the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death.”.

Industry observers note that these gloomy forecasts turned out to be dead wrong. Between 1950 and 1990, wheat yields in many countries — rich and poor — doubled, as did the yields of other crops: the fastest improvement to farming efficiency ever seen. This explosive growth, enabled by advances in breeding together with mechanization and the wider adoption of fertilizer, is referred to as the “Green Revolution.” Norman Borlaug, an American agronomist often called the father of the Green Revolution, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work. In 2009 the director of the World Food Programme stated that Borlaug “saved more lives than any man in human history.”.

Borlaug didn’t discover anything new — he just implemented existing techniques better than anyone had before. In 1944, he joined the Mexican Agriculture Program (an initiative founded and funded by the Rockefeller Foundation) under which he produced about 6,000 new crosses over a decade, a huge quantity at a time when most breeders managed fewer than 200 per year. This quantity was essential to generating the high-performing outliers that could become popular new varieties. It is even more important when two traits you want (like yield and gluten content) are negatively correlated: The more varieties you test, the likelier you are to find one that bucks the trend, performing well on both.

Rather than approaching yield directly, the program focused on two main limiting factors: wheat rust and lodging. The intensive program of crossing and selecting made it possible to develop varieties that carried several forms of resistance to rust at once, and crossbreeding with Japanese “dwarf” wheat varieties, which were shorter and more robust, produced plants that could be juiced up with fertilizer without collapsing. By the 1960s, Borlaug had produced wheat varieties that had it all: resistance to lodging, multiple resistance to wheat rust, and high yields.

In a recent development, one way this breeding program differed from previous ones was that it was split between two separate regions. The original purpose of this was to squeeze two growing seasons into one year, halving the time it took to produce a new generation. After producing the first generation of offspring in the Toluca highlands, west of Mexico City, Borlaug moved the plants north to the lower-altitude Yaqui Valley, then produced the second generation in time to move back south for the following year. In these stages, selection was crude: Only varieties that failed to germinate or were affected by rust were culled. But later stages of the breeding program included yield trials and statistical selection methods.

Alternating between two regions had another, perhaps serendipitous, benefit.8 By advancing candidates that survived in both locations, Borlaug had selected those that could perform well across different environments. Selection for photoperiod-insensitive seeds (those able to mature in both despite differing daylight exposure) meant that varieties developed in Mexico might be successfully grown in other countries, and therefore could be shared across the world. Not all plants, and certainly not all wheat, can be photoperiod insensitive, but varieties tested by the Mexican Agriculture Program were, which may explain why wheat was the first crop to flourish in the Green Revolution. Maize, for example, is so sensitive that breeders operate semi-independent breeding programs for different latitudes.

If Ehrlich was aware of this work when he predicted mass starvation in 1968, he cannot have known its significance. In the mid-1960s, India and Pakistan began importing Borlaug’s new wheat varieties. One descendant of these imported wheats (called Kalyan Sona or “golden savior”) performed extremely well and became one of the most commonly planted varieties in the region. From 1965 to 1975, wheat yields in India and Pakistan nearly doubled;9 production increased so much and so quickly that there were shortages of labor for harvest. Over time, other less developed countries followed a similar path.

The next stage of plant breeding was identifying specific genes for the precise properties that farmers wanted. The problem was that genotyping and genome sequencing were expensive and slow. The first genome was sequenced in 1977, but it belonged to a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria) with a genome nearly a million times smaller than a human’s. Sequencing the first human genome cost somewhere between $300 million and $3 billion, and was achieved much later. And this was just a diploid human genome. Wheat has a genome five times larger than that, partly because of its three hybridized subgenomes.

Breeders came up with a comparatively quick and dirty solution: marker-assisted selection. Instead of tracking genes directly, they used much cruder tests to find genetic features (“markers”) that correlated with given traits. One technique was restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, in which scientists use enzymes to chop DNA into pieces and then literally measure how long the resulting fragments are by how promptly they are pulled through gel by an electric current. While breeders would not know which genes were responsible for traits, they would know that a trait was correlated with a particular pattern of fragment lengths when cut with a particular enzyme.

Recent findings suggest that despite the crudeness of the method, it still worked for some traits, especially simple ones like rust resistance, which is often controlled by one or two genes. This allowed farmers and breeders to work out whether a variety was going to be good without going through a whole season of growing, as Norman Borlaug had to. This marker-assisted selection for many crops became routine in the 1990s. Field trials remained important, but most strains were filtered out at the marker identification stage, and few ever made it to the field. At the beginning of the decade, only a few hundred markers were known, but by the end, this had expanded to thousands.

Early marker-assisted selection was of limited use for traits like yield, which are influenced by thousands of genes. But we are no longer restricted to looking at a small number of genetic markers. DNA sequencing costs have decreased by a factor of 100,000 since 2000. Now breeders will often use “genomic selection”: essentially, using the entire genome as a marker and letting statistical software predict which genomes are associated with different traits. Genomic selection can tell us if 500 different genes each contribute 0.2% to a trait where traditional marker-assisted selection would have been useless.

This has revolutionized the process of plant breeding — if not the outcome.10 Global crop yields continue to increase at a steady rate, reflecting the fact that progress is getting harder to come by. We can now use the same genetic prediction tools for complex traits, like yield, grain quality, and drought tolerance, that we once did for simple ones. At the time Norman Borlaug was working, it took months or years and thousands of wheat plants to evaluate a new variety’s performance. Today, it can take just days to germinate a seedling and make predictions based on a small leaf sample.

Sources indicate that pessimists would say that wheat domesticated us, that we have spent thousands of years in backbreaking labor serving its reproductive ends. Optimists would argue our coevolution has benefited humanity far more, liberating us from a state of subsistence and creating a caloric surplus to sustain the lives of billions.

The human species used to live hand to mouth: Virtually all our labor was devoted to growing and harvesting food to fend off starvation. Now, in most developed countries, only a tiny fraction of the population works in agriculture. Wheat’s astonishing success is a crucial part of this change. It is the most widely grown crop on earth, covering 1.5% of the planet’s total land area, and is responsible for one-fifth of the world’s calorie intake. But the amount of labor required to produce those calories has decreased enormously. Since 1900, despite the world’s population increasing more than fourfold, the price of wheat is roughly a quarter of what it was.

That transformation is the result of sustained, incremental improvement to yield, to pathogen resistance, to ease of harvest, to taste, to gluten content, and much more. The advancements came from early farmers unknowingly favoring larger seeds; from finicky varieties that couldn’t handle frost, drought, and other hardships being killed off by the elements; and from breeders making active choices about what traits they wanted to cultivate, increasingly backed by the might of modern science. Today, we can sequence wheat’s entire genome and select for exactly the traits we want. Advances in breeding mean that similar stories can be told for every other major crop and farm animal. Each of us now enjoys the fruits of these advances at every mealtime.

Industry observers note that A lot has changed since the first wheat was farmed in the Fertile Crescent. But Enki is just as correct now as he was thousands of years ago: We would have no Sumer without grain.

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:.

The naive way is fine for 3Ã3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Î(n!) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big nÃn matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time (there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. Itâs like a determinant without any subtraction:.

Sources indicate that unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. In fact, finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is in a complexity class thought to be even harder than the NP-Complete problems; it is #P-Complete. This is composed of the hard counting problems, such as #SAT which asks how many different variable assignments satisfy a SAT formula. The counting analogue of P vs NP is FP vs #P.

What the Anthropic proof that VPâ VNP means is that there is no way to find the permanent if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:.

According to recent reports, what does this imply about P vs NP? Now for P to equal NP, one of two things must be true. Either a fast algorithm for the 0/1 permanent exists using AND/OR/NOT gates (which implies FP = #P) or counting problems are harder than deciding problems. A small intuition against the latter is that the recent resolution of the ETH skipped subexponential SAT and went right to subexponential #SAT.

#132295. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Industry observers note that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics tech giant. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

In a recent development, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

Recent findings suggest that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” claims Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Sources indicate that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

According to recent reports, the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Recent findings suggest that remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

Industry observers note that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

It has been revealed that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

It has been revealed that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just massive enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Fresh York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In a recent development, in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics manufacturer XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

Sources indicate that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” claims Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

According to recent reports, surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Industry observers note that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

In a recent development, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

According to recent reports, in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

In a recent development, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

It has been revealed that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

According to recent reports, but sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more key than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell states. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

In a recent development, during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” states neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Industry observers note that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, claims experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu states.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” claims neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Recent findings suggest that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra claims, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra indicates. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell states. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

It has been revealed that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, A few months after my visit, Remedy revealed US $62 million in newly introduced funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

According to recent reports, sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he states. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga states they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How rapidly are doctors picking up on this fresh technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Sources indicate that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

According to recent reports, X is rolling out its first parental controls, for teens aged 13 to 17. A parent or guardian can see how much time a teen spends on X and set a daily limit. They can also approve new followers and limit the For You feed to accounts the teen already follows, according to X’s Help Center.

Parents can also filter words, turn off sensitive media, and choose who can message the teen. They can see which accounts the teen chats with one-to-one, but they cannot read those messages.

Mridul Singhai, X’s product engineering lead, framed the feature around the teen’s privacy, as Tom Warren reported for The Verge.

In a recent development, “Parents get guardrails, not a window into their teen’s private life. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families,” Singhai said.

It has been revealed that the parent starts the link from Parental Controls, and X reveals a QR code and a link. The teen scans the code or opens the link and sees what the parent will be able to do. Then the teen accepts or declines. An invite expires after 72 hours.

Industry observers note that A teen can have one supervisor at a time, and a parent can supervise up to five teens. X uses the birth date on each account to decide who is an adult and who is a teen. X may also ask some consumers to prove their age with a selfie check or an ID check.

The daily limit is set in 15-minute steps. Once a teen reaches it, X locks for the rest of the day and resets at midnight local time.

Parents cannot see searches or viewing history, post as the teen, or sign in to the account. Every change demonstrates up in an activity log that the teen can also see. A teen can ask to end supervision, but the parent decides.

Michael O’Herlihy, X’s head of safety, stated the tools balance what parents and teens need, Digital Trends reported.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow,” O’Herlihy said.

Sources indicate that X admits the platform is not aimed at children. Teen accounts already run in a protected mode, which restricts sensitive media and blocks targeted ads, The Verge reported. Rivals such as Instagram’s teen accounts and TikTok have offered similar tools for a while, according to Digital Trends.

Industry observers note that the controls arrive days after Virginia and Oregon sued Musk’s SpaceX over Grok’s sexual deepfakes. In September, Ireland’s media regulator opened an investigation into X’s age checks. The regulator also questioned whether X’s parental controls met minimum requirements, Digital Trends reported.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may remember that Apple made a seeming mistake in the user interface for macOS 26, meaning that attempts to resize windows would often fail. The reason for this has now become clear, and Apple has done something both fun and clever in macOS 27 to resolve it ….

In a recent development, I was one of a number of people to note that trying to grab the corner of a window in macOS Tahoe in order to resize it would often fail. Developer Norbert Heger pointed out this is because Apple changed the radius of the corners without changing the grabbable area.

According to recent reports, it turns out that my initial click in the window corner instinctively happens in an area where the window doesn’t respond to it. The window expects this click to happen in an area of 19 × 19 pixels, located near the window corner. If the window had no rounded corners at all, 62% of that area would lie inside the window. But due to the huge corner radius in Tahoe, most of it – about 75% – now lies outside the window.

It has been revealed that at the time, the radius change itself looked like an inexplicable mistake on Apple’s part, and the manufacturer did revert it. However, Macworld’s Michael Simon appears to have discovered the reason for the original change.

The newly introduced rounder corners on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR are basically a perfect match for the macOS 26 radii.

Sources indicate that so if you move a window to the corner of the new machine, it would fit perfectly. However, since Apple reverted the corner radius, it would no longer do so. The firm solved this by a clever UI transition.

It has been revealed that what’s happening there is Golden Gate’s 20-point corner radius is subtly and gradually expanding when It approaches the bottom corner of the screen to match the exact corner of the display, which is much larger. I can’t be certain it’s exactly 26-point, but it sure looks like it to me. The effect is incredible. I’ve watched it like 20 times and I can barely see it changing, yet when it reaches the corner it’s perfectly expanded to match.

According to recent reports, you can see this illustrated by a GIF in the Macworld piece. While the original change annoyed me, Apple’s solution is the perfect example of the firm sweating the details.

  • Recent findings suggest that this shift changes how devices are designed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Recent findings suggest that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

The best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

One of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which released the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

It has been revealed that the Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

Industry observers note that it is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

Recent findings suggest that the data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

Amazfit indicates that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking revision.

The most significant change is that there's a upcoming, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

According to recent reports, I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

These practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out new AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

Industry observers note that live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they said). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

Honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a upcoming edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest update this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the latest health and safety features that are the headline.

In a recent development, the Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's newly introduced "Health Guardian" suite.

According to recent reports, technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

Industry observers note that what I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

According to recent reports, the newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

It's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

If you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

Sources indicate that not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

Last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review.

Apple didn't release a new budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

Read our full Apple Watch SE 3 review.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful revision from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

Read our full Apple Ultra 4 review.

The Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review.

According to recent reports, the CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

Industry observers note that we reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

Sources indicate that we look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility issues with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

Sources indicate that so we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the organization says you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

Over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

It has been revealed that in the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

Recent findings suggest that it's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health glitch does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a fresh smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

It has been revealed that there are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

According to recent reports, and that's one of the other substantial choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Industry observers note that fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

It also supports Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive, and a native 144Hz refresh rate, along with gaming features such as AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and variable refresh rate. That remarked, you don't have to go quite this massive to get these features, as Costco is also discounting the 75-inch U65 Pro to $699 (from $899) and the 65-inch version to $529 (from $749). The latter is particularly worth considering, having earned an "outstanding" rating and an Editors' Choice award from PCMag.

According to recent reports, ultimately, the choice comes down to whether you'd prefer the extra screen space of the QD7 or the more advanced picture technology of the U65 Pro. Either way, these Black Friday discounts make a massive-screen upgrade considerably more affordable for Costco members.

Microsoft has explained more about why it took so long to resolve the issue and mentioned that it’s urgently working on newly introduced approaches to resolve any future incidents in less than an hour ….

The senior execs responsible for the service told staff that it was the most customer-impacting incident ever experienced, and has acknowledged that not only was the problem itself unacceptable, but so too was the time taken to resolve it. Reuters got sight of a memo sent to the team.

It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday. Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to Silver’s memo.

One reason it took so long to work out what had happened was because the diagnostic data needed was “scattered across fragmented internal systems.” The memo claims 11 separate Teams chats exchanged more than 11,000 messages as they struggled to work out what exactly had gone wrong.

Microsoft is now working on five interrelated approaches to achieve a target resolution time of less than an hour for any future incidents of this nature.
