💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, neuralink has received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to start a pivotal trial of its brain implant in people with ALS, the company stated on Wednesday.
  • In a recent development, A pivotal trial is the late-stage study a company typically runs before asking the FDA to clear a device for sale.
  • Sources indicate that the study will test whether people with severe paralysis caused by ALS can control digital devices by thought, with a focus on independence in daily life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, neuralink has received approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to start a pivotal trial of its brain implant in people with ALS, the company stated on Wednesday. Neuralink calls the LINK Pivotal Study the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US.

In a recent development, A pivotal trial is the late-stage study a company typically runs before asking the FDA to clear a device for sale. The approval lets Neuralink run that study. It does not authorise wider use of the implant.

Sources indicate that the study will test whether people with severe paralysis caused by ALS can control digital devices by thought, with a focus on independence in daily life. It will also keep checking the system’s long-term safety and reliability across several clinical sites, Neuralink said.

We’ve received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.

Recent findings suggest that those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more: https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR https://t.co/Vor7iXXCBA.

Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026.

The trial follows Neuralink’s early feasibility studies in the US, Canada, and the UK. More than 30 participants have received the implant so far and have used it for thousands of hours, according to the company.

Enrolment is open to adults in the US with ALS, Digital Trends reported. Neuralink’s earlier studies also took people with spinal cord injuries or a brainstem stroke. Each participant gets the implant from Neuralink’s R1 surgical robot. They then attend about 24 months of follow-up visits, some of them remote. Neuralink has not stated how many people it will enrol.

The startup has raised more than any of its rivals. It closed a $650 million round last year at a $9 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported, citing the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Sources indicate that the road here has had problems. Neuralink’s first participant ran into major technical issues with his implant in 2024, The New York Times reported, though he said he had no regrets. In 2022, the manufacturer faced a federal investigation over its animal tests, Reuters reported.

It has been revealed that competition is growing in the US and abroad. Paradromics put its chip into its first patient in June. China approved a commercial implant the same month and implanted its first patient in July.

Beijing now wants to leapfrog the US by setting standards for brain-computer interfaces and widening their real-world use, the South China Morning Post reported on Thursday.

  • It has been revealed that “We made a billing mistake at launch of GPT-6.2 that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most consumers.
  • In a recent development, openAI will not charge users for the difference on past usage, Sottiaux said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, openAI indicates it made a billing mistake when it launched its new models, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Its fix means paying ChatGPT people will hit their usage limits faster. Compared with last week, the same work will reach the limit 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol. OpenAI executive Thibault Sottiaux confirmed the fix on X on Thursday, as Business Insider reported.

It has been revealed that “We made a billing mistake at launch of GPT-6.2 that incorrectly discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage for most consumers. We’ve fixed this now, so the same work will use more of your strategy’s usage allowance,” Sottiaux wrote.

In a recent development, openAI will not charge users for the difference on past usage, Sottiaux said. Both models launched on 17 November.

“As a small token to apologize for the mistake, we’ll be adding one banked reset for everyone on Go, Plus, Pro, and Business,” he wrote.

In a recent development, other models are not affected, Sottiaux said, according to Neowin. People should still get more out of GPT-6.2 than out of GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, he added. OpenAI’s pricing pages did not change, the site added.

Reddit customers reacted with scepticism, TechRadar reported. One user called a single banked reset “pretty thin” as an apology. At launch, OpenAI had remarked both models would let users get more done within their usage limits.

Sources indicate that usage costs are a problem across the industry. Musk has stated Grok Bot’s costs were unsustainably high relative to revenue, Business Insider noted.

In a recent development, the fix lands a day after OpenAI began merging ChatGPT’s Chat and Work tabs for some Pro consumers. Under the fresh system, both will draw on a single usage allowance, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch.

Industry observers note that most people should not hit their limits more often, the spokesperson said. A small share of the heaviest users may. Chats with the Instant model stay unlimited and do not count towards the shared allowance. OpenAI looks to roll out shared limits more broadly in December, according to its support page.

OpenAI also gained a new hire from Anthropic on Wednesday. Thariq Shihipar, who left Anthropic in October, said he has joined OpenAI. He named Sottiaux and Cat Wu, Claude Code’s former product lead, among his new colleagues.

I’m very proud of my time at Anthropic, and I’ll continue to root for my former colleagues. Both companies have notable roles to play in the future.

Industry observers note that there is a tremendous amount of work ahead of us to bring AI to the world, and it will demand the very best of all of us. I felt that I could personally contribute the most to this effort at OpenAI.

I believe this is one of the great strengths of Silicon Valley, the flow of ideas and people.

I’m excited to join a team I’ve long admired, building incredible AI products for over a billion people, and to work alongside friends like @_catwu, @thsottiaux, @ajambrosino, @sharifshameem, @jxnlco and many others to push the frontier forward.

More than anything, I hope to make your experience of using AI just a little bit better.

I am once again at your service.

Thariq (@trq212) November 25, 2026.

OpenAI’s Andrew Ambrosino welcomed him on X, writing that it is now “time to reinvent Codex”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with iPads running the same chips as Macs, many have wished Apple would give us the option of running macOS on them instead of the somewhat clunky iPadOS windowing system. Apple’s previous arguments against converging devices have been somewhat weakened by the launch of the touchscreen MacBook Pro.

A new report notes that Apple already has iPads running macOS internally, and that work on a giant iPad continues, but don’t hold your breath for a public launch of either ….

Sources indicate that as iPad hardware has grown more powerful over the years, the software has struggled to keep up. We saw split-screen capabilities first, with full windowing finally coming to the devices in iPadOS 26 last year.

The UI is still rather clunky compared to macOS, however, leading a significant number of people to wish that Apple simply offered the option of using the more powerful operating system on its tablet devices.

I would be comfortable with 11" and 13" devices running macOS. Actually, I don’t require them to run macOS itself, but I do need them to run macOS apps. I wish the iPad could match a MacBook’s productivity. Running macOS on an iPad seems like a reasonable idea. The MacBook Air is now the better price choice, while those needing a powerhouse will always choose a MacBook Pro or Studio.

Sources indicate that some suggest that running macOS on iPad would reduce Mac sales, but I disagree. I own a nearly full-spec MacBook Pro 16" and expect to keep a machine like that, yet I also purchased a MacBook Air for lighter travel. I would prefer an iPad over the Air, but I cannot choose it because it lacks the apps I require. If it supported them, I would buy the iPad Pro with all accessories, and Apple would gain more revenue from me. I appreciate the concept of owning an iPad, but at the moment it lacks the value needed to justify paying more for a device that simply does less than a MacBook Air.

In a podcast Q&A, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says that Apple is already doing this internally, but there’s no sign of any plans to make it available outside the organization.

In a recent development, apple has iPads internally running macOS, and they’ve had that for some time. The fact that they have the underlying architecture of Apple Silicon that’s the same on the iPad and the Mac gives them the flexibility in order to test these types of things.

Recent findings suggest that in terms if they’re actually going to do it – would they bring macOS to the iPad itself – at this point I don’t think that’s going to happen anytime soon. I’ve checked into this and there’s no ongoing operating system project right now in terms of a brand newly introduced operating system for the iPad – there is no work being done to consumerize macOs on the iPad.

Gurman notes Apple seems set to continue to make piecemeal changes over time to bring iPad capabilities closer to those of the Mac but is showing no signs of full convergence.

He reiterated that work on a long-rumored giant-sized folding iPad continues.

The other thing I want to say is that I’m really excited for this potential of Project J312. That is, this giant 19-inch, 20-inch foldable iPad. And it’s basically like a gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside.

It has been revealed that however, he notes there’s no guarantee it will ever launch, saying the timings have already slipped from 2027 through 2028 to 2029, but both cost and yield complications may still kill the project. If it does launch, it’s expected to cost anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s Voyager building at its headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
  • Sources indicate that S&P Global Ratings has put Nvidia’s AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade.
  • Any cut would likely be a single notch, to AA-, S&P remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s Voyager building at its headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Sources indicate that S&P Global Ratings has put Nvidia’s AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade. The Jensen Huang saga exposed weak spots in how the organization is run and overseen, the agency noted in a note on Wednesday. It could cut the rating within 90 days if those problems remain.

Any cut would likely be a single notch, to AA-, S&P remarked. It could go further if investigations or disclosures showed harm to Nvidia’s reputation or future business. The watch covers both the manufacturer’s rating and its senior unsecured debt.

“News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in NVIDIA’s management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness,” S&P wrote.

In a recent development, the agency stated the long tenure of some directors may have compromised their independence. Nvidia’s governance may also not have kept pace with its fast growth, it added.

“While NVIDIA management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the ‘key man’ risk to the forefront,” analysts Andrew Chang and David Tsui wrote.

S&P cut its management and governance score for Nvidia to neutral from positive. Huang’s departure and his reinstatement do not answer its questions about how the board oversees executive conduct, it mentioned. The agency intends to meet the board and management to discuss board independence, oversight and a credible succession initiative.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s competitive position, technology lead and finances are unchanged for now, according to S&P. Stricter export controls could still slow its growth. The agency would take a harsher view if it came to believe Nvidia broke or got around export rules. The same goes for any sign that past disclosures understated its exposure to China and nearby regions.

S&P’s move follows Moody’s. On 18 November, Moody’s lowered its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive over governance concerns, CNBC reported. Moody’s kept that outlook after Huang returned. Nvidia shares have fallen about 12.5% since Monday’s close, CNBC added.

A lower rating could raise Nvidia’s borrowing costs. The firm sold $25bn of senior notes in June, shortly after S&P raised it to AA, according to CNBC.

Nvidia also lends its AA rating to less creditworthy companies by backing their debt, leases and hardware purchases, Semafor reported. On Wednesday, measures of credit risk for Nvidia and CoreWeave hit record highs, Bloomberg reported, as fears over AI debt returned.

Some critics say the agency is late. Nvidia had no board chair until Huang resigned on 12 November and Harvey Jones became its first, Martin Peers wrote in The Information. That weakness was public in Nvidia’s filings, and S&P could have flagged it earlier, he argued.

The Bank of England says the way the AI boom is financed is making the global financial system more fragile. AI financing is taking a form that is “increasingly complex, circular and opaque”, the central bank warned. It set out the concern in its Financial Stability Report on Thursday.

That makes it more likely that stress in one market spreads to others, the Bank stated. Higher interest rates and rising sovereign debt add to the pressure.

“Taken together, these developments heighten the risk that multiple vulnerabilities crystallise simultaneously,” the Bank’s Financial Policy Committee wrote.

Hyperscalers, the few tech groups that run giant data centres, are set to glitch more than $305bn of bonds this year. That is around 8% of global investment-grade issuance, according to the report. Some AI companies also fund others in the sector against future revenue commitments. Such circular deals make it harder to see where risks sit, the Bank mentioned. The IMF raised the same worry about circular AI deals in October.

Sources indicate that hyperscalers now have links to the financial system of around $4tn, Bloomberg reported, citing the review. Katharine Braddick heads the Bank’s regulatory arm. She told reporters that supervisors want to stop any fall in AI values washing “back through the banking system”.

The Bank also flagged rising cyber risk. Frontier AI has kept advancing since July, especially AI agents and open-weight models, it said. Recent incidents showed how hard it is to stop autonomous agents acting against what developers and users intended. Open-weight models are cheaper to run and their safeguards are easier to remove, which could help attackers.

It has been revealed that recent Google Cloud and Microsoft outages revealed how one provider’s trouble can hit many firms at once. Further ahead, quantum computing could break widely used encryption, so a move to quantum-resistant cryptography is now a priority. The Bank is setting up a Systemic Resilience Council of industry figures and officials to coordinate its response, Bloomberg reported.

According to recent reports, lenders are already shifting some of that risk. Citi and JPMorgan are marketing portfolios of AI-related loans, people familiar with the deals told Semafor. Some banks want to manage risk, while others want room to lend more.

Sources indicate that some deals use synthetic risk transfers. These keep the loans on a bank’s books but pass the risk of losses to investors. Banks are joining hyperscalers, which already move debt off their balance sheets, Semafor’s Ellen DiMauro wrote.

In a recent development, the borrowing is not slowing. JPMorgan strategists expect $450bn of investment-grade AI debt next year, up from $368bn in 2026, Bloomberg reported. That comes as fears over AI debt return to markets.

Sources indicate that the Bank still judges UK banks well capitalised and able to keep lending in a much worse downturn. It completed its review of bank capital rules on Thursday. Under the review, Tier 1 requirements for major UK banks will fall by about 50 basis points of risk-weighted assets.

“Reducing capital requirements much further would risk financial instability,” the committee added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

According to recent reports, data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” claims Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Recent findings suggest that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The manufacturer’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Sources indicate that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” notes Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Fresh Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

In a recent development, back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Industry observers note that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon notes this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the company’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon states. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”.

Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

In a recent development, the startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the firm’s tech to beat GPUs.

According to recent reports, instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr states.

Sources indicate that to accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the manufacturer is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

Industry observers note that “The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

Industry observers note that the approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The tech giant is at the moment choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr notes. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

In a recent development, free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another major advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” notes Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

It has been revealed that in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the company revealed a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main glitch is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch states, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Industry observers note that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Sources indicate that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

The Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” states Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the organization’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to swiftly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

LightSolver’s team is at the moment working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the company’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi indicates. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

Yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick Upcoming, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

According to recent reports, the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Fresh indicates. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

Sources indicate that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

It has been revealed that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Fresh says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he indicates. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Claims Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Industry observers note that whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” indicates Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print concern as “The Return of the Optical Computer.”.

  • Many investors were no doubt pleased with Anthropic's public debut, but individual retail investors aren't the only ones to benefit.
  • Industry observers note that what's more, Alphabet has significant cloud computing and processor deals with Anthropic, further entangling the two companies' futures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Chris Neiger – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:00AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) recently completed the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, raising $81.3 billion -- beating the previous record set by SpaceX by $6.3 billion in June.

Many investors were no doubt pleased with Anthropic's public debut, but individual retail investors aren't the only ones to benefit. Alphabet (GOOGL -2.13%) (GOOG -2.02%) holds nearly 14% of Anthropic's shares, making it one of the largest shareholders in the artificial intelligence (AI) firm.

Industry observers note that what's more, Alphabet has significant cloud computing and processor deals with Anthropic, further entangling the two companies' futures. Here's how Alphabet and its shareholders benefit from the recent Anthropic IPO.

Starting in 2023, Alphabet made a series of investments in Anthropic over multiple funding rounds that eventually totalled about $33 billion. At the time of Anthropic's IPO, Alphabet held 13.7% of Anthropic's stock.

That investment was a very wise move, considering that Anthropic's shares were priced at $83 at the IPO, making Alphabet's position worth about $149 billion. Of course, as Anthropic's shares rise and fall, the value of Alphabet's stake shifts.

Industry observers note that holding Anthropic's shares boosts Alphabet's reported net income on paper each quarter (if Anthropic's returns go up), without generating actual cash. Alphabet could eventually sell some of its Anthropic shares to reinvest in the manufacturer, but it's likely to hold on to them, or at least the bulk of them, for a while.

If Alphabet holds onto its stake, it could add significant unrealized gains to its reported income. When it sells some of its shares, it will directly benefit shareholders by providing fresh capital for growth or buybacks. So, even though Alphabet and Anthropic compete with their AI models, Alphabet shareholders will still benefit as Anthropic grows.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Sources indicate that anthropic said in its S-1 filing before going public that it had about $121 billion in spending committed to Google between April 2026 and July 2033. The good news for Alphabet was that Anthropic was locked into that spending "regardless of actual usage.".

What's more, Anthropic also buys Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) for AI processing. The AI company will reportedly spend $2.5 billion on Google's TPUs this year and up to $7.2 billion next year.

Altogether, Anthropic is estimated to spend up to $200 billion on Google Cloud and TPUs over the next five years.

Sources indicate that with Anthropic being a core Google Cloud and TPU customer, its financial stability is a good thing for Alphabet. Now that Anthropic has raised more than $81 billion from its IPO, the deals between the companies are essentially de-risked because it can use the proceeds to pay for some of its commitments.

According to recent reports, and Anthropic could expand its deals with Alphabet in the future, as demand for its services increase. Anthropic's third-quarter revenue rose 47% to $17 billion, indicating that the firm is already on the right growth trajectory.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Recent findings suggest that alphabet is positioning itself well in the AI era as the company expands sales of its TPUs and grows its Google Cloud service. Morgan Stanley estimates that Google could generate $84 billion in graphics processing unit (GPU)-related sales next year alone. That would be an enormous opportunity for the company, considering that it only just began selling TPUs to customers earlier this year.

In a recent development, what's more, the tech giant's Google Cloud revenue is rising fast and more than doubled in Q3 to $30.7 billion. The company ended the quarter with $561 billion in Google Cloud backlogs, 55% of which management notes will be fulfilled over the next 24 months.

While Alphabet certainly benefits from its significant stake in Anthropic, I think the company's growth from Google Cloud and massive opportunity from selling TPUs make it a compelling AI stock on its own.

And given that Alphabet's shares trade at just 15 times the company's trailing earnings -- compared to the tech sector average of about 24 -- the company's stock looks like a good buy right now.

Sources indicate that this is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

(Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.

Sources indicate that android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

In a recent development, graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS.

Industry observers note that GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Appleâs mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the âclassicâ Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic.

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon.

Recent findings suggest that neXTSTEP was NeXTâs influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

Apple Newton was Appleâs PDA launched in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

In a recent development, palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palmâs mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS, covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

Style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI, or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

Sources indicate that taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

According to recent reports, does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6, and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

In a recent development, thatâs it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • WhatsApp has started rolling out scheduled messages, which let consumers write a message now and have it sent automatically at a later date and time.
  • Industry observers note that to schedule a message, consumers press and hold the send button in a chat and choose a date and time.
  • Users can schedule text, photos and videos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WhatsApp has started rolling out scheduled messages, which let consumers write a message now and have it sent automatically at a later date and time. The Meta-owned app declared the feature on 25 November and calls it one of its most-requested features.

Industry observers note that to schedule a message, consumers press and hold the send button in a chat and choose a date and time. Messages can be set between 10 minutes and 14 days ahead, and the feature works in both one-to-one and group chats.

Users can schedule text, photos and videos. Pending messages can be viewed and deleted at any point before they go out, and they arrive looking like any other message.

Scheduled messages are still end-to-end encrypted, so WhatsApp cannot read them. They also send at the chosen time even if the sender’s phone is switched off or its battery has run out.

In a recent development, the feature is reaching owners globally over the coming weeks. WhatsApp did not say whether it will reach Android, iPhone and the desktop apps at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that the launch follows months of testing. WABetaInfo, which tracks WhatsApp test builds, first spotted the feature in development in February. It reached a small group of Android beta testers in October, before arriving for some iPhone testers.

It has been revealed that during testing, scheduled messages were kept in a dedicated section of each chat’s info screen, WABetaInfo reported. Testers could attach only one photo or video per scheduled message, and recipients were not told that a message had been scheduled. Deleting one before it went out did not notify them either.

Industry observers note that rival messaging apps have offered similar tools for some time. Telegram already lets users schedule messages, and Apple has offered a Send Later option in its Messages app since iOS 18. Google Messages also supports scheduled texts.

According to recent reports, until now, WhatsApp consumers who wanted to send a message later had to rely on reminders or third-party tools. Businesses that use the app to take orders from retailers have also built their own workarounds on top of it.

The app passed three billion monthly owners in 2025, according to Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. India and Brazil are its largest markets, by number of users.

If you want the most portable way to listen to music on the go, then the best earbuds are a fantastic way to do it. They're tiny, often comfortable, and offer noise cancellation to keep the sounds of the outside world at bay.

At the moment, the AirPods Pro 3 take the crown. But we've spent hundreds of hours testing earbuds to find out which are the best around if you want more than just Apple's offering. They come at a range of different price points to suit any budget, too.

According to recent reports, each entry on the list has a quick read section, giving you a brief overview of the buds, followed by longer reviews so that you can get a better idea of how they perform. So let's get straight into it. These are the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

We've spent 20 years testing the best earbuds (and the worst; you don't know until they're in your ears) to help you find your next set of portable audio companions.

The expertise comes from a few places, including our expert reviewers Erin Bashford and Nikita Achanta, who lead our audio testing. Then there's me, Tammy Rodgers, and I've been testing audio equipment for over half a decade, including a time as Tom's Guide's Audio Editor.

Before any earbuds make their way to this guide, here's how we put them through their paces to make sure we only recommend sets we truly believe in and would use ourselves.

Recent findings suggest that when you're looking for new earbuds, there's a whole range of terminology brands will use to talk about specs and performance. To make things a bit easier, these are the most common terms that come up, and what they mean for you.

Most earbuds come with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It uses audio magic and some very clever algorithms to quiet the outside world and make your commute more manageable.

The earbuds have mics on the outside to pick up external noise. As this passes into your ear, the earbuds generate an opposing frequency to cancel the sound before you hear it. Sometimes this can change the sound of your music, so we'll report when the ANC is either too weak or too invasive.

It has been revealed that the EQ, or equalization, allows you to customize the way the earbuds sound. Usually, this means a series of sliders or dials in the companion smartphone app for adjusting the bass, mids or treble. Some manufacturers give you preset EQ options, which save you from getting lost in sliders or graphs.

These are the different sounds that make up your music. You'll generally see them divided into three simple sections: the lows, the mids, and the highs. The lows are the bass frequencies. Think bass guitars and kick drums. You want them to be impactful and low.

Industry observers note that the mids are the main parts of your music, like vocals, guitars, and synths. Because they're so important, you want them to be thick and wide. Finally, the highs are cymbals and other higher sounds. These should be crisp and clear.

It has been revealed that tammy is one of Tom's Guide's Buying Guide Editors. She also spends a great deal of her time testing the best earbuds, evaluating them for sound, ANC, comfort and battery life. She's always got at least three pairs of earbuds to choose from at her desk.

Sources indicate that erin is a proud music nerd and needs the best earbuds around. Whether it's eardrum-shedding nu-metal or tranquil folk, she'll listen to it. If a pair of earbuds has awesome sound quality, bouncy ANC and are comfortable? It's an immediate recommendation, regardless of price or brand.

In a recent development, as a music nerd, Nikita is always listening to music. As a reviews writer, she tests earbuds by pushing battery life to the limit and analyzing performance across various genres to answer the question: Are they good value for money? She listens to music almost throughout the day and plays guitar and bass, so she knows how to determine whether a pair of buds reproduces sound well.

Recent findings suggest that why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Sources indicate that the AirPods Pro 3 are the latest version of Apple's popular flagship earbuds. The stem-like design remains, but you get better battery life, an improved fit and more detailed sound. This makes them a worthy upgrade from the AirPods Pro 2, and the gold standard for wireless earbuds. Plus, the Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate monitor and Live Translation (if you have a compatible iPhone).

Sources indicate that the AirPods Pro 2 were excellent, but soon aged out compared to the competition. Now, the AirPods Pro 3 have arrived to conquer all and lay waste to Sony and Bose. And, despite a couple of minor flaws, they're currently the best wireless earbuds you can buy right now.

Recent findings suggest that these are the very best earbuds that Apple has ever made. They've got some key updates over the previous model, for one. There's the extended battery life of eight hours, improved sound quality, and superior noise canceling to keep the noise of your commute at bay.

It has been revealed that those upgrades have materialized in a pair of buds that stun in sound and make sure that your office is a whole lot more tolerable when you're getting on with your day. They lose out to the Sony and Bose due to a lack of codec support for Android devices, but there really is nothing better if you're an iPhone user.

According to recent reports, the AirPods Pro 3 improve on the old model in the sound department. They've still got Apple's more neutral sound signature built in, but find more detail and extra bass depth than the older pair.

They've got a very solid soundstage as well. They're on par with the Sony buds, and better than the Bose alternatives — although there are still options out there that sound better.

Spatial Audio for movies with an Apple TV is still a great way to watch your content, and just as easy to connect up. It works well for music as well, especially when you listen to your music on Apple Music.

It has been revealed that the buds have been shrunk this time around, and as a result, have a very comfortable fit. The silicone eartips have been infused with foam for a softer and more comfortable finish, and they mold better to the inner part of your ear.

In a recent development, that means you can wear them for extended periods of time. The sweat and water resistance means you won't have to worry about wearing them when you go to work out, either, hitting an IP57 rating this time around.

The AirPods Pro have always had 'good enough' ANC; powerful but not exceptional. But that changed with the Pro 3, which now almost compete with the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2, but don't quite beat out Bose's buds.

In a recent development, still, it's very good and blocks out all the major noises of your commute or your busy office. It's on par with the Sony WF-1000XM5 — both are excellent noise-canceling options.

Transparency mode is very good as well, and boosts the battery life by another couple of hours. Nice.

There isn't an app for the AirPods Pro 3, but you can easily adjust their settings from the iPhone settings menu. There, you'll find all their features along with options to patch the firmware and change the sound.

Industry observers note that although you can pair the AirPods Pro 3 to an Android phone, I wouldn't really recommend it. You get the bare minimum on a non-Apple phone; a wireless connection. You can't adjust settings, so I'd only suggest the AirPods with an Android phone if you're in a bind.

Much like on the Apple Watch, the battery life for the AirPods has remained stuck for years, allowing the competition to lead ahead. The AirPods 3 Pro buck the trend and, for once, increase the per-bud battery life up to eight hours of ANC listening.

That's a two-hour increase and puts them almost in line with the Sony and Bose sets. If you switch over to the transparency mode, you get 10 hours of battery life, more than pretty much anything else at their price point. That also means you can use the new Live Translation feature for longer.

According to recent reports, the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds boast excellent sound quality, customizable EQ, and great battery life. Noise cancellation excels, and the design is also great. These are a highly recommended upgrade for superior quiet and sound control.

When following up on a highly successful pair of earbuds, there are a couple of things you do. First, you make things better — more features, better sound quality. Then you improve the design — make the fit better, improve the looks.

That’s the WF-1000XM6, Sony’s follow-up to the WF-1000XM5. The AirPods of this generation make a better case for your money if you wield an iPhone, but the XM6 are great for just about everyone else. Just like their predecessor, they’re a fantastic all-rounder, with great specs, sound and ANC.

In a recent development, our four-star review highlights that they’re not entirely perfect. The newly introduced case design is a bit odd and makes fitting them into a pocket a chore, and they’re more expensive than the previous model, but those are our only major criticisms.

The sound quality is, as you might expect for something from the WF-1000X series, very good, with support for LDAC. Sony’s excellent DSEE Extreme audio upscaler is here as well, and works a treat. The ANC boasts a massive improvement, too, although Bose still has Sony beat for out-and-out noise performance.

They’re a wonderful pair of comfortable buds with plenty of battery life — there’s little more you could ask for, apart from a discount.

Sources indicate that they may seem on the expensive side, but the upgrades in sound performance make them totally worth it. Sony is known for a warmer sound profile on their headphones, and these are a total joy to listen to.

They are only made better by using the personalized EQ settings on the earbuds, and there’s seriously no genre that these buds can’t cope with.

Your favorite songs will sound a lot more detailed, and it’s really awesome to get a studio sound from earbuds instead of having to rely on studio headphones to do the job.

Recent findings suggest that these earbuds are superbly comfortable, and you get a bunch of different eartip options in the box to get the best seal and best security. You can do a fit test to make sure everything fits.

I can wear these buds for hours at a time — they’re seriously comfortable, and they’re lightweight so they never weigh me down.

ANC differs depending on personal experience with these buds. My own experience was amazing, and I couldn’t fault them at all. They made a long travel day on a plane, train, and bus completely silent.

Industry observers note that however, another one of my colleagues who tried them out was still able to hear the sounds of traffic moving around. I think it’s all about the eartip fit, so this is an extremely crucial process to complete.

If you buy this set, just make sure you use the Optimal Earbud Tips feature in the Sound Connect App to get the best fit, and ensure your ANC is working properly.

Sources indicate that the Sound Connect app is one of the most user-friendly I’ve tried. Once you get the hang of things and organize the app to suit the settings you need to use the most, it’s incredibly handy and makes using the earbuds so much better.

The app is where you do all the earbud fit tests and personalized EQ tests to make the overall experience with the buds so much better.

Industry observers note that you get eight hours of battery per bud with ANC and 24 hours with the charging case. This is pretty standard and matches up with Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 and the Sony WF-1000XM5.

The A100 SE are all about sound — pure and simple. There's no feature bloat, no extra AI things, just a pair of great-sounding earbuds with epic battery life. The ANC has fallen behind the competition a little this time around, but they're a great pick for a fantastic price.

It has been revealed that the first Cambridge A100 are some of my favorite wireless earbuds — and the SE version are no different. They come in at a price that doesn’t break the bank and offer some of the best sound quality around. For sub-$150, they sound better than buds that cost twice as much — there’s a reason we constantly compare them to the AirPods Pro 3 and others in the review.

Industry observers note that they’re refined and classy in their sound, as befits a legacy British Hi-Fi brand. The soundstage is expansive and well layered, and vocals shine. Erin loved the dynamism and vibrancy in her review, noting the accuracy and faithfulness of their representation. High praise indeed.

We had no problems with the comfort as well, and wore them extensively during the testing period. The case is compact and well-shaped (perfect for fitting them into a tighter pocket), and the app is useful and well laid out, though simplistic.

According to recent reports, there are just a couple of problems. The ANC isn’t quite up there with other options at a similar price, and the Dolby Atmos mode is, like, bad. But beyond those two bugbears, the A100 SE are the perfect successor to some of our favorite earbuds and a top-notch value pick.

Sources indicate that cambridge has fired a warning shot at just about every other audio manufacturer with the A100 SE. The first model sounded good, but these sound even better. We love how dynamic and clear the buds sound, and the seven-band custom EQ means you can really dial them in.

They sound better even than more expensive earbuds, and take the fight to options that cost $100-$150 more. That’s the focus of the buds: excellent sound, forget the frills.

There’s warmth here, but it doesn’t overshadow the rest of the sound. Everything is still very clear and expansive, with solid instrument separation. We’re substantial fans of the sound.

We scored the buds well for comfort, thanks to their smooth shape and range of different eartips. For the most part, we were able to wear them for long periods without them getting uncomfortable. We didn’t want to rip them out after the workday.

It has been revealed that but those with small ears might struggle a little more. These aren’t small buds, and for one tester, they pressed on some parts of their ear. They weren’t uncomfortable, but they knew they were there.

According to recent reports, the ANC isn’t going to win them any awards. It’s fine and blocks out some noise, but it’s not as all-encompassing as other options available. If you’re looking for something that blocks out everything, then you might want to think about Sony’s similarly priced options.

Still, if ANC isn’t a priority but you still want some noise blocking, then you won’t find anything to complain about — and the noise-canceling compromise is worth making for that excellent sound.

Cambridge’s app is fine, but we did have some problems with some of the features. It became a little buggy at times, with some features not working as they should. A quick restart fixed the matter, but it’s still worth mentioning.

What we really liked, however, was the complete omission of extra feature bloat. There’s everything you might need — an EQ, ANC controls, and that surround mode — but there’s nothing extra. No AI feature, no voice control thing, just what you actually need when using the buds. That’s refreshing.

Battery life is a particular strength of Cambridge's headphones and earbuds. Here, we’ve got 39 hours on tap, 10 hours of bud life. That’s more than just about anything else out there, including buds that cost a whole lot more. It even takes some over-ear headphones to task, and they generally have buds beat for staying power.

Everything charges up promptly, and we found that the battery figures matched up to expectations when we did all of our testing. If you want something that lasts a long time, the A100 SE are a great option.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are the fitness lover's dream. A very comfortable, secure fit so that they stay in place no matter how you move around, and great sound quality to power your workouts. The built-in heart rate monitor is a great cherry on top.

It has been revealed that now, I'll be the first to admit that I'm not a fitness expert — but I sure am an earbuds expert. As earbuds, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are great. They've got excellent ANC from the AirPods Pro 2, and there's some great sound for a solid audio experience.

According to recent reports, given that I'm not a fitness expert, I also spoke to someone who is, so that we can get a picture of why they're on the list. From my review, our fitness expert Nick mentioned:"I genuinely believe that the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are outstanding sports headphones and would be top of my list for people who need an earhook to keep their buds in place during runs and other workouts.".

It's thanks to those secure-fit hooks that keep the earbuds in place no matter how much you run or move around. The heart rate monitor is a nice extra, but we were slightly disappointed with its accuracy.

For all kinds of exercise, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are an excellent earbud option for everyone.

Industry observers note that while not high-fidelity, there's a rhythmic energy to the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 that's infectious. They've got some great bass presence, as you might expect, but they're also good in the upper register too.
