The battery life of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 is exemplary. They feature 10 hours of battery life in the buds themselves, beating out many other options on this list.

According to recent reports, that's perfect for long-distance runners and cyclists, or gym-goers who want something that will take them to the gym, last through their exercise, and then take them home again. We found those battery life claims were true in our review. Pop them in the charging case for 45 hours of staying power.

Sources indicate that improving on almost every metric compared to the original model (except battery), the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2 are an in-ear noise-canceling triumph. Boosts to ANC and sound quality make them an even better buy than the first model, and the price hasn't increased to match the improved performance.

The QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds were my favorite release of 2024, and the Gen 2 are now my favorite of 2026. They've improved on pretty much everything over the first model, with the only exception being the unchanged battery life — but it's that world-silencing ANC that really takes them over the edge.

They remain the very best way to listen to music without disruption when you're traveling. That busy train carriage? Silenced. The office? Quietened completely. With that signature orchestral swell, you're in your own world, free to listen to your tunes.

Sound is much better this time around, although you'll still want to adjust the EQ in the Bose app. And you'll be listening comfortably for their entire 6-hour battery life thanks to their incredibly comfortable fit.

Industry observers note that I gave them 4.5 stars when I reviewed them, thanks to that all-conquering ANC and solid sound quality. They lose out in the battery department to the XM6, opting instead for out-and-out ANC performance — and there's nothing better to block noise.

The bassy sound of prior Bose earbuds is still here, but it's been refined slightly this time around. There's more detail retrieval, and the soundstage has been extended, but the bass weighting is still very much present.

I've found that dipping into the Bose apps' EQ is a must with any of the brand's headphones. From there, I adjust the bass down slightly and the highs up a few notches to increase the detail and reduce any muddiness. They sound great out of the box, but these improvements make them sound even better.

In a recent development, there's also Immersive Audio, Bose's spatial audio setting. Some like its ability to make music sound much larger, but I find it thins out notable frequencies. It also tanks the battery by two hours, making them last an even shorter time.

Yeah, they're still some of the most comfortable buds you can buy. I've been able to wear them for hours and hours at a time without the need to adjust the fit or take them out for a break — they're a lovely thing to have in your ears.

Industry observers note that it's all down to the fitting options. There are loads of different silicone tips, and the fit is further improved by the rubber fins you can attach to the edge. They're secure as well, so they won't fall out should you get headbanging or dancing.

It has been revealed that the ANC is the best around — there's nothing that comes close. That's high praise given how good the previous model was at keeping out unwanted sounds, but Bose has somehow made it even better. It's a bit like magic.

You can choose different levels for the noise canceling, but I prefer to leave it on the top level. That way, I don't have to worry about any noise making its way through at all, and I can enjoy my music to the max.

Bose's app is one of the better options around. It's very well laid out, and everything is clearly labeled so that you don't get confused. It even demonstrates you what's playing, although I'm not entirely sure how useful that feature is.

Sources indicate that it's where you'll find all of the EQ options, noise control, and different sound modes. I particularly like how the app knows what color your buds are — and even lets you name them.

In a recent development, battery life remains a weak point in the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2's armor. We've still only got six hours' worth of life here, which pales in comparison to some of the competition.

The WF-1000XM6 last for eight hours, a whole two hours more than the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. You can't even turn the ANC off to boost the battery life — six hours is all you're going to get.

It has been revealed that the Noble Fokus Amadeus are all about one thing and one thing only — their sound quality. Sound quality that blows just about everything else you can buy out of the water. Their ANC is very good, and they're very comfortable, but you buy these for their sound quality.

The Noble Fokus Amadeus are not cheap. They're $70 more than the AirPods Pro 2, and $50 more than the XM5 and the QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds. They're not the most expensive earbuds around, but you should be ready to shell out if you want a pair.

And you will want a pair, because they've dethroned other excellent-sounding earbuds with their incredibly well-rounded sound signature that dishes out masterful amounts of detail while providing plenty of low-end punch.

According to recent reports, for the price, this is about as close to wired earbuds as you're going to get. The crisp detail is utterly sublime, their mids are fat and juicy, and the bass is tight, controlled, and impactful. An audiophile's wireless dream, one might say, and the upcoming earbud sound quality standard that all else must be measured against.

Sources indicate that the price means they're out of reach for many customers, but as I discovered in my testing, they're well worth their higher price thanks to a very good all-round package. The battery is good, and the ANC matches up — there's very little to get sad about here.

The absolute best thing about the Noble Fokus Amadeus is their sound profile. Thanks to the Audiodo profile in the app it means they sound amazing for everyone too, catering the sound for specific hearing needs.

Recent findings suggest that there are details in my tracks I'd not heard for a while thanks to the impressive detail, and the mids bring plenty of body to listening. The bass kicks and barks with impressive control, notably adding more for drum and bass in particular.

Industry observers note that the sound is effortlessly spaced apart for a wide soundstage, and the instruments are very well separated. They sound better than absolutely everything on this list — they're hard to get hold of, but it's worth every single effort when you do.

The Amadeus come with a range of different fitting options in the box for a very comfortable fit. They're more shaped and molded than other options as well, making them easier to wear for longer periods of time.

My favorite fitting options are the flanged tips because they not only improve the sound and the ANC, but they stay in place better than the other options.

While not quite as good as the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, the ANC is still very good, especially if you opt to use the included flanged tips. It blocks out plenty of noise, focusing on low-end sounds like bus engines.

Recent findings suggest that transparency mode is nice and natural as well, and makes it easier to talk to shop clerks and bus drivers without needing to take buds out of your ears. There's perhaps a little more noise than some might like, but it's otherwise very good.

The Noble Fokus app is very simple and lacks some of the more in-depth modes and settings of some of the competition. It's very easy to use, though, and offers everything you actually need.

There's the Audiodo sound customization, as well as a very in-depth EQ to really dial the sound in to your preferred listening curve. You can also change the noise-canceling mode and adjust the volume. Beyond that, there's not much else. At least there's a nice picture of your buds.

Battery life is very solid in the Fokus Amadeus. The buds last for eight hours with the ANC turned on, and 12 hours if you turn the ANC off. They charge swiftly in the case, which provides a total of 42 hours of charge. That's amongst the very best battery life on the list.

Wireless charging is the cherry on top, and a 10-minute quick charge for two hours of use is a nice bonus too.

Recent findings suggest that CMF's latest pair of budget buds are sub-$50 heroes. They pack in loads of premium features, like great customization and even a form of spatial audio. They sound great, fit well, and come in a range of different colors. What's not to like?

In a recent development, this is a spot that’s likely to be occupied by CMF for some time — the brand's budget buds are just that much better than everyone else's. For just $50 (and often less thanks to significant price drops during deal events), you get earbuds that feel like they’re worth a whole lot more.

CMF has packed in a whole range of great features. There’s sound customization from Dirac, which generally deals with premium Hi-Fi equipment. You get a form of spatial audio to make your music sound bigger, and there’s even great ANC to keep the outside world at bay.

It has been revealed that the sound is the most impressive thing here, though. They sound like a pair of buds that cost loads more, and once you’ve gone through the Dirac sound tuning, there’s very little better for under $100. Premium buds — low price.

Sources indicate that thanks to CMF’s use of Dirac, the CMF Buds 2 sound excellent. While the core sound is very good, with plenty of bass for impact and revealing detail for interest, the EQ settings kick things up a notch. We’ve described it as “breathing newly introduced life into your songs” — and you’d be hard-pressed to find something at this price that sounds better.

Recent findings suggest that they’re great for a wide range of genres as a result. We spun up everything from the heaviest of metal to breezy folk and classical, and the buds didn’t skip a beat. They’re as meaty as they are delicate — extremely impressive considering the price.

There’s nothing else that sounds like this at the low price point at which they sit. Even without Dirac, they’re impressive — although you’ll want to run the tuning engine to get the most out of them possible.

Thanks to a multitude of fitting options in the box and a great bud design, the CMF Buds 2 are very comfortable. There are three different sizes, and we found that the ‘small’ size option was perfect for even very small ears.

There are comfier buds out there, but we had little problem wearing them all day during our testing. More expensive buds might feel slightly nicer in the ear, but these still feel great for the price.

You can’t expect Bose-level ANC for $50, but you’ll be immediately impressed by the noise-canceling packed into the CMF Buds 2. It does a very good job of keeping the outside world at bay, with some very impressive noise blocking.

The transparency mode is good too, making it easy to hear what's going on without a robotic edge. They cut down slightly with the ANC during calls — while your voice will be clear, your call partner will be able to hear everything going on around you.

It has been revealed that the Nothing X app is excellent. It's super simple to navigate, with easy access to all the features in the buds. There’s a home screen, and then various menus that are clearly labelled. It’s a must-install if you pick up the CMF Buds 2.

This is where you find the Dirac tuning menu, as well as other settings. Those include the ANC settings, fit test, spatial audio, and touch control settings.

11 hours of use in the buds is very solid indeed, and our testing showed no reason to dispute CMF's claims. The case contains 55 hours of use, so you can charge the buds about four times from empty. This is good battery life for buds, better than even some of the more premium options.

Samsung's latest buds bring a less AirPods-like case design and excellent sound quality to the table. Some settings and options are locked off for everyone but Galaxy device users, but they're a great option for the Samsung faithful.

Not one to miss out on a good earbud battle, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro bring a whole host of features to the Samsung crowd who want something that seamlessly integrates with their phone.

Industry observers note that they sound great, and Samsung’s audio upscaling tech is almost as good as Sony’s for improving weaker streams from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music. That looks like the place Samsung has put the most work into the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro, improving massively over the older model.

Industry observers note that not quite as much work seems to have gone into the battery life, unfortunately. There are only around seven hours on tap with ANC turned on, which lags behind the key competition like the eight hours of the AirPods Pro 3. Still, you get more charge in the case at 30 hours.

Samsung has also packed in some very solid ANC, with loads of clever modes if you wield a Galaxy handset. That’s where their true value lies. There are a bunch of features that only Samsung customers will appreciate, like AI translation that only works with Galaxy phones.

Industry observers note that if you’re a Galaxy phone user, then the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro were likely already on your shortlist. Thanks to our testing, we can tell you that they’re a great pair of buds that’ll pair with your device perfectly.

“Overall, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound utterly divine” is how Erin finished off the sound portion of the buds review. That’s thanks to rich bass, excellent mids, and great vocals, giving you a top-notch audio experience.

Detail heads might prefer the slightly tighter AirPods or Sony WF-1000XM6, but these sound better than the likes of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds Gen 2. Their AI sound enhancement works great with lower-quality streams as well.

Thanks to some solid shaping, the Buds 4 Pro are comfortable to wear for long periods of time. There are plenty of fitting options in the box as well to make sure that you’ll find the best fit for you, no matter what shape your ear canals are.

Some with smaller ears might find their slightly larger bodies tighter, but it’s not enough to make them in any way uncomfortable.

The noise canceling is excellent, blocking out all the noise that we could throw at them. They perform about the same as the AirPods and Sony competition, making for more relaxing journeys while wearing them.

Recent findings suggest that transparency mode is also good, and doesn’t make any of the incoming noise sound robotic. The ANC performance might not be quite as impressive as the Bose buds, but it’s more than a match for the Sony and Apple alternatives.

Some of the headline features, like the AI settings and call enhancement, are only available for Galaxy S23 models and newer. The buds use the Samsung settings menu itself rather than a dedicated app on these devices, and it works well.

Industry observers note that there is a Samsung app for other devices, and it's fine. You can control the ANC and other settings, and update the firmware. Still, there are better app experiences for non-Galaxy people, like the Sony and Bose apps.

Battery life is fine. It’s not as good as the eight hours you get from the AirPods or the Sony WF buds, but the seven hours on tap is more than enough to get you through the day. The 30 hours in the charging case, though, make up for the slightly lacking battery life of the buds.

It has been revealed that not every pair of earbuds we test can land on the best list — otherwise, this would just be a list of earbuds that are available to buy. But some are still pretty good and worth considering if you need more options.

Thanks to some key upgrades (mostly in the sound department), the AirPods 5 are a great pair of earbuds, especially with the fresh lower price compared to the AirPods 4. The battery life just isn't good enough, however, and compatibility with Android remains an glitch that holds them back from a full-chested recommendation.

Recent findings suggest that the EarFun Air Pro 4 bring some excellent features at a bargain price. For a lot less than $100, you get solid ANC, great sound, and a very comfortable fit. They last for ages thanks to their 7.5-hour per-bud battery life, and support loads of hi-res codecs so that your music always sounds its very best.

Read our full EarFun Air Pro 4 review.

The Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 are wonderful earbuds with impeccable sound and a monstrous 52-hour battery life. But the ANC isn't as effective as we'd like, and the case is large and cumbersome to carry around.

Read our full Cambridge Audio Melomania M100 review.

Sony's WF-C710N are well-priced buds that bring some great specs to the table and don't cost the earth. Their ANC is solid, and the sound is very good. We found them comfortable to wear for long periods of time. Whether you like the transparent blue design will probably help you decide if these are right for you.

Read our full Sony WF-C710N review.

The Liberty 5 Pro Max are Soundcore's first entry into the premium earbud space. It is largely successful, with good sound and solid ANC. But at this price, the AirPods Pro 5 or Sony WF-1000XM6 are better value for immersive audio with ANC.

Read our full Soundcore Anker Liberty 5 Pro Max review.

Before we make a recommendation about any pair of wireless earbuds, we want to make sure that we've put them through their paces. It helps us find out how good they'll be when you find them in your hands, and makes sure that we can pen our informative, buying advice-packed reviews.

Industry observers note that it's all work — no fun. Listening to our favorite music for hours on end to test the sound, taking the earbuds out and about on day trips to test their long-term comfort and ANC algorithm. In all seriousness, we put a lot of effort into making sure that you'll be happy with a purchase you make after reading our buying guides and reviews.

Here are the key factors in our testing and how we evaluate each pair of earbuds that falls across our desks.

In a recent development, earbuds are going to be jammed directly into your ear holes, so one of the most notable things that we test is how comfortable they are over long periods of time, and how difficult it is to dial in the fit. How many bud bits do you get in the box, and are they easy to fit on the buds? Are they loose? Are there extra fitting options like earhooks?

Recent findings suggest that to find out, we put the buds through their paces. We try out a range of the tips that come with the budsto find the perfect fit that makes the ANC excellent and sound good. After all, if they don't seal well inside of your ear, you're not going to get the best out of your buds. We report our findings, like how easy it was to get the perfect fit, and how comfy they are when dialed in.

Then we test their long-term comfort. That means wearing them for hours during a work day, so that we can see how they feel when they're worn for hours on end. If they start impacting certain pressure points in the ear, we'll notice, and it'll go into our review. We're looking for earbuds that can't be felt during wear, so that you forget you're wearing them.

It has been revealed that this is my favorite thing to test. Hours and hours of my favorite tunes played into my ears while I work, and I don't have to make excuses to my boss about why I need to be doing it. Excellent news. When we test the audio quality of a pair of buds, we play the Tom's Guide testing playlist on Qobuz so that we can get a good picture of how they sound with some top-quality hi-res tracks to put them through their paces.

Industry observers note that we listen at first in a quieter environment so that we can get an idea of how they sound in a vacuum without the ANC to cause potential problems. We compare the earbuds to the sound profiles of those in the best list above, and then we write down our findings for the full review.

In a recent development, then, we take the earbuds out with the ANC to see if it changes the sound. It might all sound like we're having fun, but there is a point to it all. It gives us a clear picture of the buds' performance in an everyday use case, so that we can see how they'll serve you if you decide you'd like to buy a pair.

Pretty much every pair of earbuds that you can buy today comes with some form of ANC (unless you buy some of the very cheapest ones at the very end of a lengthy Amazon search, you madman), and we want to make sure that it performs well in a variety of use cases.

How do we do it? By taking the earbuds with us wherever we go. That could mean on all our daily commutes, to see if they perform well on the train, or out for hikes so we can see how well they handle normal atmospheric noise. Maybe we're going on a flight — then we can test how well they handle loud engines and crying children.

Once we've thoroughly tested how much noise they block, we also test the transparency modes when we go to buy our tickets or a bag of candies from the grocery store. We look out for how clear the voice of our conversation partner is, and whether they're audible through any other noise. We're also looking out for the quality of the audio that's being pumped in. Is it too loud? Again, we note down our findings for the review.

Industry observers note that finally, we want to make sure that the ANC doesn't change the sound of the music too much. After all, you want your music to sound great, and if the ANC changes things too much, it can create annoying sonic concerns.

In a recent development, given that your earbuds are often going to pull double duty as a form of hands-free calling system, we want to ensure that they're going to be good at it. We make a whole bunch of calls to check things out.

We're looking out for a couple of different things. First of all, we want to make sure that we can hear our call partner well, and that they're coming through clearly. We listen out for clarity and judge whether we can hear them properly throughout the duration of the call, and whether their voice sounds natural.

According to recent reports, then we ask our call partners how we sound. Can they hear us properly, or do the noises of our environment make it hard to hear what we're saying? We note down our findings, and then we report back on them in our review to give you an idea of how they'll perform if you want to take (or make) a call.

According to recent reports, we know that manufacturers sometimes have a habit of overestimating their battery life figures. To make sure that you're getting the best information possible, we spend the time testing the battery life claims and whether they ring true. We listen to the buds for hours on end, and count how many hours we used them before they needed to go back into their case. We do this with ANC turned on and with the volume at a comfortable level.

According to recent reports, for charging cases and very long-lasting buds, we extrapolate battery data in a different way. We measure how long we've used them, and then compare that with how much life we've got left. This gives us a good picture of how the battery is going to last in the long run, and whether you'll get those rated claims.

Sources indicate that hopefully, we've managed to curate a list of wireless earbuds that hit the mark for you. But if you're still not sure how to choose between them, these are some additional pointers.

What do you want out of your buds?

There are as many reasons to buy earbuds as there are earbuds themselves. You need to work out what you're looking for first and foremost — it's why I've divided the list up into the most important headline features.

Do you want the best sound, and would you be willing to give up some battery life and pay a bit more for it? If not, then you should go for the best earbuds overall, but if you don't mind some compromise, then you should go for the best-sounding earbuds.

It has been revealed that it's important to make a list of the features that are most important to you, and then work out from there which of the earbuds on the list fit those criteria the best. After all, what might be the best for one person might not be the best for you.

Do you want headphones or earbuds?

If you're looking for the most compact, easily transported audio device around, then the best earbuds are probably going to be right for you. But there are a couple of things to remember: they're going to live inside your ears, and not everyone likes the feeling of in-ears after longer periods of listening.

Recent findings suggest that if you'd prefer something more comfortable for longer periods of wear that offers more battery life, and potentially better audio quality, you should consider some of the best wireless headphones. They might cost a bit more, but you might be more comfortable.

Repairability is becoming ever more notable, as we try to find new ways to lengthen the life of our devices, but also look after the planet that we call home. Repairing products is great for both, and it's important to consider it when buying new tech.

Unfortunately, earbuds are one of those products that are extremely rarely user-repairable. Thanks to their size and the amount of tech that companies have to pack into their buds, it's generally impossible to make the insides accessible to you or me.

Not all is lost, however — some manufacturers do offer some form of repair service, so you don't have to worry if your buds stop working. But this is still pretty rare, so if this is a priority for you, it's worth picking up a pair of the Fairphone Fairbuds 2.

Recent findings suggest that there are seven user-repairable components; they cost less than $100 and come in two colors. Tom's Guide Managing Editor James Frew rated the first generation, but they weren't available in the U.S. That all changed with the Fairbuds 2, which you can buy directly from Fairphone.

It has been revealed that I talk about this on our best headphones list, but I think it's worth reiterating here. It's easy to get hooked on frequency response graphs and numbers, and think you're getting a surefire cheat code to finding the best-sounding earbuds.

You'll spot them as a pair of numbers in spec lists, like "15 Hz-22 kHz." The first number is how low the earbuds can go, and the second is how high they can go.

You might think that finding a pair with the greatest frequency range is going to net you a pair of excellent-sounding earbuds. While that can be true, it's not worth seeking out. Just because a pair of earbuds can go really low doesn't mean they're good at replicating those frequencies, and neither does it tell you about what's going on in the music itself.

It has been revealed that there's only one way to really tell how good a pair of earbuds is — and that's to give them a listen. Or, of course, you could read one of our excellent and informative earbuds reviews.

In a recent development, minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.

Sources indicate that minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Strategy 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.

Recent findings suggest that the demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.

Recent findings suggest that the demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.

A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.

In a recent development, in CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:.

The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.

Sources indicate that exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.

Sources indicate that the source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:.

Sources indicate that minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.

45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.
  • Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall.
  • If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.

Sources indicate that SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

We also saw a lot of newly introduced companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with significant industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.

Industry observers note that the real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Recent findings suggest that rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our newly introduced cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

According to recent reports, water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal.

In a recent development, the same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

Recent findings suggest that designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the newly introduced set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

In a recent development, at SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

Recent findings suggest that my instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing indicates 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®.

FinVolution (FINV -2.02%) reported a sequential contraction in loan volume as management prioritized asset quality and funding stability amid regulatory and institutional shifts in the Chinese market. The manufacturer stated that its diversification strategy successfully used growing international operations to offset domestic headwinds, with overseas revenue increasing to 37% of the total mix. In China, management responded to a tightening institutional funding market and reduced collection capacity by restricting credit to high-quality existing borrowers and upgrading risk models. Operational progress continued in international markets, including Indonesia and Australia, where the company expanded its offline presence and utilized open banking data to refine credit pricing. FinVolution maintained a liquidity position of RMB 8.4 billion while continuing to return capital through share repurchases and the retirement of convertible debt.

For nearly a decade, we have spread our business across markets, economies, and regulatory regimes not because anyone of them was under pressure, but because we knew that one day, one of them could be. This quarter, that day came in China and while our domestic business absorbed the shock, our overseas business kept growing and kept they growing. Once again, diversification carried us. The third quarter was a challenging transition period for China business.

In July, a credit event at another platform eroded confidence across China's loan facilitation industry and financial institutions sharply put back funding to the sector. From late July, a nationwide campaign against collection agencies cut collection capacity and efficiency. Together, these 2 developments hit our China business on 3 fronts: advance funding supply, credit performance, and loan origination. We responded as we said we would on last quarter's call, prioritizing funding stability and asset quality over growth. We tightened underwriting and directed to funding available to us towards our best quality existing borrowers. As a result, group's loan volume contracted to approximately RMB 20 billion, down 56% sequentially, driven mainly by the slowdown in China.

Meanwhile, our diversification strategy continued to work as intended. Overseas volume grew 11% year-over-year to RMB 4 billion. Revenue rose to RMB 949 million, 11% year-over-year and 2% sequentially. Overseas now account for 37% of group revenue. More importantly, this growth is also profitable. Overseas operating profit more than doubled year-over-year to RMB 62 million. Now let me take each segment in turn, starting with Chinese Mainland. Regulation now reaches into every part of the lending process. The upcoming financing cost disclosure rules took effect on August 1 and the new online marketing rules on September 30.

Compliance is our first priority, and we have worked with our bank partners on loan products and the referral flows that meet the latest requirements. China loan volume contracted to approximately RMB 16 billion, down 61% sequentially, reflecting tighter funding supply and the elevated credit risk across the industry. On funding, institution turned risk averse from July and the supply fell sharply. Our priority throughout the quarter was to restore funding and keep it aligned with loan origination. We gave our bank partners full visibility into our fund flows and processes, and adopted our partnership model to their requirements and risk appetite, including closed-loop payment controls and additional checks.

According to recent reports, as a result, funding supply recovered steadily from its July low through August and September. Though it remains below normal level in early October, we and other lending platform also completed compliance self-checks on fund flows and submitted clean audit reports from independent third-party firms to the National Internet Finance Association of China. We believe this marks an important step in restoring institutional confidence across the industry and our compliance record positioned us well as funding partners become more selective. On risk, our metrics improved steadily throughout the first half of 2026.

In a recent development, the trend reversed in July, driven by 2 industry-wide factors: First, as funding tightened across the industry, borrowers had less access to credit and the repayment to legacy loans generally weakened; Second, the collection campaign we flagged last quarter reduced recovery capacity and pushed the delinquencies higher. In response, we upgraded our risk models and tightened underwriting further during the quarter. Our approach was simple, lend less, lend it to the people we know, and keep bad actors out. I would like to further elaborate on this in a bit. In this elevated risk environment, we expect legacy loans to continue to weigh on credit costs.

According to recent reports, looking ahead, we will maintain our compliance-first risk-focused approach through this reset in China with asset quality as the core priority. Now let's move on to the overseas segment. Our overseas business maintained its growth momentum with volume up 5% sequentially to RMB 4 billion. Our diversification markets portfolio continued to act as a buffer against country-specific headwinds. In Indonesia, Indonesia remains our largest overseas market. Offline Buy Now, Pay Later accounted for approximately 31% of volume this quarter, up from approximately 25% in prior quarter and 10% a year ago. The shift is deliberate.

Offline Buy Now, Pay Later is originated at point of sales, so the use of funds is easier to verify and the customer relationship runs through a merchant network rather than a paid traffic. With acquisition costs and regulatory scrutiny both rising, that is a more durable way to grow. In the Philippines, volume edged down 5% sequentially as the business cycled under the newly introduced rate cap. Credit performance came in better than expected, helped by another typhoon season and the conservative underwriting we put in place over the past 3 quarters. We believe the transition to the lower rate cap is largely complete, and we look to restart growth in the coming quarters. In Australia, volume grew 21% sequentially.

In a recent development, the growth came with a better customer mix with higher quality middle to large loans rising to around half of the portfolio. The key was the deeper integration with Australia's open banking regime, which gave us verified transaction level data on income, spending, and existing debt in place of self-declared inputs. That data works in 2 directions. We can approach good credit applicants we would previously have declined, and we can price and size credit limits more accurately for everyone else. As a result, conversion among good credit applicants improved while our underwriting standards held firm. On the foundation, we are now adding larger ticket products for borrowers with stronger credit profiles, and we expect the mix shift to continue.

According to recent reports, technology remains to -- how we run this business and this quarter, it mattered more than ever. As the collection campaign cut industry capacity, our AI collection agents helped offset part of the lost external capacity. Two of our AI applicants, including our customer service agent built on our own large language model, [ RAG Fin ] were also named exemplary cases in Shanghai's 2026 Collection Of Outstanding Artificial Intelligence Applicants. The agents has served more than 100 million owners with a roughly 7% relative increase in self-service resolution. To close, at the start of this year, we said we would move through 2026 with patience and caution.

Recent findings suggest that china's reset is still underway, and we expect the industry to keep evolving around risk, funding, and regulation. We expect to come through it with a clearly more resilient China business and overseas business that contributes a growing share of our profit. We entered this period with RMB 8.4 billion in cash and short-term investments and a strong diversified overseas business that continues to grow. I will now turn the call over to our CFO, Alexis, for a deeper look at the numbers.

I will cover each segment and then the group results. First, China. Our priorities this quarter were funding stability, risk mitigation, and cost discipline. China revenue was RMB 1.5 billion, down 38% sequentially, reflecting a smaller loan book, partially cushioned by deferred revenue from legacy loan cohorts. Take rate for this quarter landed at around 2.9%, down 30 basis points from the second quarter due to rising credit and funding costs.

According to recent reports, our credit risk indicators remain elevated for 2 reasons: The industry-wide funding squeeze and the collection campaign that began at the end of July. For loans originated in the third quarter, we expect vintage cost of 3.5% compared with 2.7% for the second quarter. Early risk indicators demonstrated a smaller -- a similar trend. Network delinquency rose from 5.3% to 6.4%, mainly from legacy loans originated before funding tightened. The 30-day collection rate fell from 89% to 85% as collection capacity across the industry strength. As a result, CM2 rose from 0.56% to 0.92%.

Sources indicate that as Tim mentioned, we are tightening risk controls on 3 fronts: be selective with newly introduced customers, lend to the people we know best, and shut out fraud. First, our new customers with funding tight across the industry, risk surface faster and the quality of the new customer traffic deteriorated. So we became much more selective. We tracked how stress were spread across the industry and used those signals to adjust our approval strategy and the credit limit models early. We shifted our channel mix toward higher quality source and cut off high-risk traffic. Second, our existing customers in a tougher environment, we focus on funding borrowers we know well.

But even familiar borrowers can change quickly when credit drives up elsewhere. So we looked more closely at 3 warning signs: Borrowing from multiple plans, pipe platforms, high debt relative to income, and unstable repayment. We re-evaluated the portfolio by risk-adjusted return, reduced exposure to borrowers showing these signs, and moved the credit limits to those with proven track records. We also added specific controls for borrowers who repeatedly paid a few days later and early signs of stress. This keeps our risk exposure contained. Put credit in steady hands and ease pressure on collections. Third on fraud. When credit tightens, fraud becomes more organized. First through intermediaries and the connected networks that one-by-one application checks cannot catch.

We strengthened pattern detection across money flows, intermediary behavior, application networks, and the devices. We will remain vigilant as we entered the fourth quarter and continue to prioritize loan quality. During the quarter, funding costs also rose from 3.7% to about 4.3% as the tight supply pushed up the cost of funding from a low base. We work closely with our funding partners to restore supply, while funding has not yet returned to normal level. It has recovered to a level sufficient for our current risk appetite and origination strategy. Moving on to overseas. Operating profit was RMB 62 million, up 15% sequentially and more than double the prior year level.

Demand remained resilient, and we added 2.8 million newly introduced borrowers, up 28% sequentially. That stated, the macro backdrop across our markets has become more challenging. Higher oil prices are driving inflation and monetary policy is tightening across the region. We are managing each market with that environment. In Indonesia, the rupiah has become under sustained pressure and the Bank Indonesia has raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to year high 6% to support the currency. Consumer confidence has softened with the index falling from 127 in July -- in January to 120 in October. We are monitoring credit quality closely and are ready to adjust our risk strategy early if conditions warrant.

In the Philippines, inflation rose to 7.2% in September and the Central Bank has raised 4x in a row, most recently to 5.5%. As they scaled back origination ahead of this, we are well-positioned to restart growth at a measured pace. In Australia, the Reserve Bank has raised its cash rate 5x this year to 4.85%, and though we are mindful of the pressure, this puts out household budgets. Even so, demand for digital credit adoption remains strong, and we expect Australia to keep contributing to both growth and profit. Overseas operating profit for the first 9 months totaled about RMB 161 million, and we remain on track for our full year target of about USD 30 million in EBITDA.

And at the group level, net revenue was RMB 2.6 billion, down 25% sequentially. Operating expenses were RMB 1,048 million, down 27% sequentially, mainly due to lower sales and marketing spend as we serve more repeat customers through our own app rather than paid traffic. Total provision expense was broadly flat at RMB 1.35 billion despite lower origination, reflecting higher credit costs on legacy loans. Net profit was RMB 206 million, down 52%. Our balance sheet remains liquid and strong. Cash and short-term investments totaled RMB 8.4 billion. Our leverage ratio, defined as risk-bearing loan balance divided by shareholders' equity was 1.5x, a historical low. Our shareholder returns -- our capital allocation policy is unchanged.

Our current priority is to meet the operational needs of our business while optimizing our cost of debt. We repurchased USD 4.3 million of shares in the third quarter, bringing repurchase for the first 9 months to USD 71.1 million. In October, we prioritized capital toward our convertible senior notes, repurchasing about USD 19 million, which reduces our debt and the potential dilution. We remain committed to returning capital to shareholders based on sustainable normalized earnings and cash flow. Now to our outlook. Despite the third quarter's disruptions, group revenue reached RMB 9.2 billion for the first 3 quarters.

We are, therefore, reiterating our full year revenue guidance of RMB 11.5 billion to RMB 12.9 billion and expect to land at the lower end of that range. This reflects our current and preliminary views subject to any changes to the operating environment. To sum up, the third quarter indicated both the cost of China's reset and the value of the choices we made before and during it. We cut volume early, tightened risk, and amended our funding relationships. We believe that the new environment will favor players with strong compliance discipline and operational know-how. Meanwhile, our overseas business continued to grow both its top and bottom lines.

We are clear-eyed about the domestic challenges ahead and firmly committed to disciplined execution through the coming quarters with our focus on long-term returns for our shareholders. That concludes my prepared remarks. We will now open the call to the questions. Operator, please continue.

Industry observers note that by 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].

Industry observers note that early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T unveiled newly introduced Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].

It has been revealed that for roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].

Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].

US Treasury’s FinCEN takes systems offline after a cybersecurity incident

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is investigating a cybersecurity incident and has taken some systems offline.
  • Industry observers note that “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.
  • FinCEN has not mentioned which systems the intruders reached, what data they accessed or who was responsible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Treasury Department in Washington, DC.

The US Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is investigating a cybersecurity incident and has taken some systems offline. The bureau posted an alert on its filing website on Tuesday, which The Verge first reported.

Industry observers note that “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems. As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline,” the bureau said in its alert.

FinCEN has not mentioned which systems the intruders reached, what data they accessed or who was responsible. Its Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website is still running, although some services may be unavailable for now.

What the bureau holds is sensitive. Banks and other financial institutions file suspicious activity reports with FinCEN under the Bank Secrecy Act. The bureau shares that financial data with law enforcement to fight money laundering and terrorist financing.

Industry observers note that the disclosure followed days of disrupted bank filings. Filing providers reported problems as early as 18 November, when automated batch submissions to FinCEN stopped, The Deep Dive reported. FinCEN posted an alert about a disruption to that batch service, known as SDTM, on 20 November. It has not said whether the intrusion caused the outages.

On Tuesday, FinCEN also issued a relief order. Filers now have until 30 December for reports due between 18 November and 29 December. The extension covers institutions that used SDTM as of 18 November and companies due to file beneficial ownership reports. It also covers people who must patch a FinCEN Identifier.

It has been revealed that the order blames a service disruption and does not mention a cyberattack, The Deep Dive noted. Other anti-money-laundering duties, including monitoring for suspicious transactions, still apply. Banks that need to get suspicious activity information to law enforcement quickly can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline. FinCEN says the disruption has not affected it.

In a recent development, finCEN’s alert came hours after reports that hackers had reached an unclassified CIA system. The breach, of an open-source intelligence system, also hit other spy agencies. Investigators suspect the intruders used the Artex hacking tool. It is unclear whether the two incidents are related, The Verge reported.

It has been revealed that last week, hackers also reached the FBI’s crime database, and the Agriculture Department took applications offline after a security incident. In December 2024, hackers broke into Treasury’s departmental offices through a stolen key from the vendor BeyondTrust. The department blamed a Chinese state-sponsored group.

Treasury’s chief information officer, Sam Corcos, heads the office in charge of the department’s cybersecurity. While FinCEN dealt with the incident, Corcos was pushing updates to Legatum, his open-source strategy game modelled on Civilization VI, 404 Media reported.

The game is built largely with AI coding agents, Claude and OpenAI’s Codex, according to its readme on GitHub. Corcos co-founded the glucose-monitoring start-up Levels and joined Treasury as a DOGE hire.

Latest Update: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4725 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Sources indicate that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon confirmed his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Sources indicate that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is crucial because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

According to recent reports, I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company revealed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead.

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress.

AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?

AI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.

The intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

In a recent development, claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Recent findings suggest that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

It has been revealed that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

It has been revealed that we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s crucial to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the manufacturer’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

In a recent development, using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

It has been revealed that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Recent findings suggest that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its people because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted prepares for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the organization judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Sources indicate that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Recent findings suggest that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar, Festivitas lets you hang lights of different colors and patterns from your Mac’s menu bar and dock. It has a bunch of different customization options, so you can tweak the lights to match your preferences.

Last year, the app added a latest snowfall effect alongside those Christmas lights, plus Shortcuts integration and a dedicated iPhone and iPad app with customizable widgets.

According to recent reports, this year’s Festivitas update expands that snowfall feature. Now, the snow that falls from the top of your Mac’s screen can pile up at the bottom of your screen, and you can use your mouse to shovel it away. This joins the existing ability to adjust snow amount, flake size, fall speed, and wind direction.

Head to the Festivitas website to get started and bring some holiday cheer to your Apple devices.
