I've been playing board games for as long as I can remember — about 20 years now. My first game was Scrabble, which I still play with my family and partner.

In a recent development, board games have come a long way, and they're still an excellent way to bond with your family and friends. The holidays are almost upon us, so I highly recommend grabbing either a classic or a brand upcoming one this week. As Tom's Guide's resident board games expert, I've rounded up the best Black Friday deals for you.

It has been revealed that my favorite deal is on Catan which is 51% off right now. This is a phenomenal and highly addictive strategy game for up to four players. If you want a more simple game to play with kids and adults alike, get the Magnetic Chess Game for just $8.

According to recent reports, if you fancy a card game instead, P for Pizza is my top recommendation, and you can get it for $9 today. Or if you're hosting an adults-only games night, you can't go wrong with Cards Against Humanity which is down to $23 for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that regardless of what you're into, there's a deal for everyone, so allow me to take you through the best Black Friday board and card game deals. And let me know in the comments which game you'll be playing!

By day, I review consumer tech for a living. By night, I'm playing either video games or board/card games. I've loved board and card games since I was a child. My favorites are Scrabble, Catan and Monopoly, and I also thoroughly enjoy silly card games like P for Pizza and Herd Mentality.

In a recent development, when I visited my family a couple of months ago, we spent hours playing this Magnetic Chess Game. One player makes a shape with the included string and other players must place their magnetic pieces without touching the others. It's a great game for adults and kids alike.

This is one for whodunnit and murder mystery fans. Clue is discounted for Black Friday, and is a great game to play with friends and family over the holidays. In this murder mystery board game, you and up to six other players act as detectives to solve a murder. You must figure out who committed the crime, the weapon they used, and which room the crime took place in. Other players will try to ruin your strategy by using cards in their hands, and the first person to make an accurate accusation wins.

Sources indicate that do you like board games that are equal parts visually aesthetic and fun? Try Azul! It's a tactile game about tile laying. The mosaic tiles are inspired by Portuguese azulejos. It's easy to learn and deceptively deep in strategy, and works great at just about any player count. If you're not feeling the tile laying, there's a chocolate variant and three sequels that offer different rules and shaped pieces.

I'm sure you've played Monopoly hundreds of times (just me? Okay...), but if you haven't, what are you waiting for? Monopoly's an all-time classic. You and up to five other players buy, sell and scheme your way to becoming the richest person alive. You can build houses and hotels and trade these if a player offers you a better deal. Warning: may cause (friendly) arguments!

According to recent reports, few board games come close to being as great as this one. Catan is a highly addictive strategy game for three to four players which turns you into hard-nosed settlers, competing to conquer an island. You must collect resource cards to build roads, village and cities, but collecting them heavily relies on dice rolls and trading with other players. Oh, and there's a resource-stealing robber too to spice things up, so watch out!

When we're having a cozy date night, P for Pizza is a game my partner and I always play. In this fast-paced card game, you have to shout out a word that links the letter on one card to the category on another (on a pile in the middle of the table). For example, a food that starts with G, an actress whose name begins with K, a stringed instrument that starts with S, and so on. You need to be quick to add a slice to your pile, and the first one to form a 'pizza slice' wins.

Need a party game for the holidays? Try Herd Mentality. It's easy to pick up and play as all you need to do is flip a card and read out a random question like, "Who is the most popular female artist of all time?" You and the other players then write down the answer you think will be the most common among the group. If you're in the majority, you win points; if not, you'll be left with the dreaded pink cow of doom. And as someone who adores cows, you don't want to get stuck with this one...

Recent findings suggest that if you want a fast-paced board/card game where you deduce your fellow players' behavior, The Chameleon is for you. In this game, everyone know a secret word except one hidden imposter. Each player gives a single related clue to prove they belong without revealing too much. The group then votes to unmask the traitor... or Chameleon, if you will. Each round can last as long as the group likes.

According to recent reports, the first time I played You Can't Say UMM was at a board games café with my friends. We laughed so much that our jaws hurt and we had tears running down our faces. In this card game, you have to describe an object to your teammate without saying "Umm" or "Err." The opposing team can catch you out and penalize you. Opponents can also add "rules" to your turn, such as, "Swap seats with a teammate after every correct guess." It's harder than it sounds, and it's a barrel of laughs.

According to recent reports, cards Against Humanity is the perfect card game for adults — and to determine who among your friend group has the darkest humor. One player reads a fill-in-the-blank prompt from a black card, and everyone else submits their funniest, most offensive, or absurd white answer card. The reader picks the winner, awarding a point. It can get really horrible really fast — but it's oh so fun.

Sources indicate that my partner and I play Ransom Notes with our friends fairly often. In this game, you and the other players race against a timer to answer outrageous prompts using only a limited handful of random word magnets. Everyone reads their grammatically chaotic sentences aloud while a rotating judge picks the funniest response to award a point. The first to five points (or the number of your choosing) wins!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training.

Fresh to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

Sources indicate that this option is presently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

It has been revealed that hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a new thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Also: Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills.

Certain limitations are in effect with a temporary thread. Specifically, you can’t do any of the following:.

According to recent reports, are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:.

“Temporary threads will not be saved to your Google account and disappear after 24 hours,” Google said on a support page. “They won’t be used to train Google’s generative AI models, unless you submit feedback or it’s necessary for safety purposes. Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”.

Industry observers note that google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes.

Sources indicate that for those reasons, you should still be cautious about the information you share even in a temporary thread. But certainly, this option provides greater privacy and protection than a regular AI Mode search.

It has been revealed that chatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot all offer a temporary chat mode that also promises to keep your chats private and unconnected to your account. Claude and Perplexity provide the same feature but call it incognito mode.

In a recent development, I’m glad to see Google finally offering this option through its AI Mode searches. This marks the second privacy-friendly development in recent days from the search giant. On Tuesday, Google unveiled that it would be rolling out new settings through which you could opt out of AI model training without losing access to your chat history.

#132185. This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1209 w)

This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • No, your phone isn’t listening to you.
  • Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.
  • Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No, your phone isn’t listening to you. But what about your Apple Watch? I’ve been testing new Audio Intelligence features that record conversations around me, and despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

Apple has built-in privacy safeguards for the audio, how it’s processed and then deleted. I’ve broken all that down in a separate Audio Intelligence FAQ. This is about what it’s like to use it in the wild.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple states it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they remarked than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows).

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

Industry observers note that I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

In a recent development, what it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding looks during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

It has been revealed that rather than coming away better informed about the key conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

According to recent reports, apple has quietly announced the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the firm has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac ….

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the company has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

As we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the tech giant has averaged two newly introduced stores a year.

It has been revealed that india has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

Additionally, India does not allow firm-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

The blueprint worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each upcoming store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

According to recent reports, to download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.

It has been revealed that linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

Industry observers note that so too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this new take on the OS is the epitome of that.

The distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with new ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”.

In a recent development, the developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

The Pond UI consists of the following:.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend.

If you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:.

Pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind.

At the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a new workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Sources indicate that pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:.

Recent findings suggest that once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

It has been revealed that as I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One matter that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI update system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:.

According to recent reports, I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an patch component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux.

It would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

In a recent development, you should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my latest favorite free productivity suite.

Sources indicate that pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Trade Desk (TTD +0.14%) finished 2025 at $37.96 a share, off about 68% that year.
  • Unless shares rise about 170% before the year ends, the ad tech firm is headed for back-to-back losing years for the first time since it went public in 2016.
  • Industry observers note that since 2017, its first full year of trading, the stock has ended every year higher except 2022 and 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 3:43AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than The Trade Desk ›.

The Trade Desk (TTD +0.14%) finished 2025 at $37.96 a share, off about 68% that year. At roughly $14 as I write, the stock has fallen another 63% in 2026.

Unless shares rise about 170% before the year ends, the ad tech firm is headed for back-to-back losing years for the first time since it went public in 2016.

Industry observers note that since 2017, its first full year of trading, the stock has ended every year higher except 2022 and 2025. It dropped around 51% in 2022 and then rose about 61% in 2023.

Sources indicate that this history makes a 2027 bounce tempting to expect. But the business is in a very different spot than in 2022, and so is the stock's price.

It has been revealed that the Trade Desk's revenue rose 32% in 2022 to about $1.58 billion, and fourth-quarter revenue grew 24% to a record $491 million. Free cash flow (the cash from its operations after paying for equipment and software) climbed about 43% to around $457 million.

The stock still fell, along with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -0.62%). The index sank 33% that year as the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates to curb inflation and growth stocks lost favor.

Even after the drop, the stock finished 2022 at around 48 times The Trade Desk's free cash flow for the year. The sell-off mainly shrank a high valuation, but the business itself kept expanding.

Industry observers note that the rebound came the same way. In 2023, revenue climbed 23% to around $1.95 billion, the Nasdaq surged 43%, and The Trade Desk's stock gained about 61%.

The 2025 drop didn't track the market. The Nasdaq climbed around 20% that year, but The Trade Desk's stock fell 68%.

Sources indicate that it tracked the company's results instead. Revenue growth went from 18% in the third quarter of 2025 to a 0.5% drop in the third quarter of 2026, even with a one-time lift from business with a strategic partner. The fourth-quarter forecast calls for revenue of at least $755 million, around 11% under last year's $847 million. Reaching that floor would put 2026 revenue at about $2.9 billion, flat with 2025.

According to recent reports, profits are shrinking faster. Third-quarter net income dropped about 67% year over year to $38 million, partly because of $44 million in charges linked to cutting about 15% of its staff. And management forecast fourth-quarter non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) of at least $280 million, down from $400 million a year earlier.

The tech giant's latest quarterly filing says third-quarter revenue fell partly because existing clients spent less and partly because it gave bigger discounts on joint business aims and other partnerships meant to fuel future growth. The bigger discounts look like a company trying hard to stop ad dollars from moving to Amazon and Google parent Alphabet, whose ad businesses The Trade Desk CEO Jeff Green calls "walled gardens.".

The price is the other big difference. Cash and short-term investments totaled about $1.6 billion as of Sept. 30, and The Trade Desk had no debt. At roughly $14 a share, the whole company is valued at about $6.7 billion, so the cash covers about a quarter of the price. The board also boosted its buyback authorization to $1 billion this month.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

According to recent reports, free cash flow for the last four quarters was $847 million. So the stock costs around eight times the company's yearly free cash flow.

Sources indicate that A 61% gain from here would send the shares to about $23. Even then, the stock would cost only about 13 times the company's free cash flow for the past year.

That free cash flow number will probably fall when this year's weaker fourth quarter replaces last year's. But I don't think The Trade Desk needs anywhere near 2023's 23% revenue growth for the stock to do well. It mainly needs sales to stop shrinking.

It has been revealed that I doubt it. The 2023 gain rode a business growing over 20% and a market rebounding with it, and the organization's own forecast still points to shrinking sales.

But with shares trading around eight times free cash flow, I'd consider owning the stock without a repeat. I'd keep it to a small position for now and add when revenue grows again.

#132178. Porch Pirates Don’t Care About Your Doorbell Camera. Follow This Expert Plan Now

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1231 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Porch Pirates Don’t Care About Your Doorbell Camera. Follow This Expert Plan Now

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Doorbell cameras may seem like a good way to make a porch thief think twice, but the reality doesn’t quite match up.
  • That’s the case for my fellow CNET editor, Gael Cooper, who had her Amazon delivery stolen a few weeks ago and spotted the thief on camera.
  • According to recent reports, “When Amazon emailed me that the order was delivered and it wasn’t there, I was very confused,” Cooper said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Doorbell cameras may seem like a good way to make a porch thief think twice, but the reality doesn’t quite match up. Some porch pirates don’t care about being caught on camera as long as they’re able to steal your package, and it’s unlikely that law enforcement will track down the stolen goods.

That’s the case for my fellow CNET editor, Gael Cooper, who had her Amazon delivery stolen a few weeks ago and spotted the thief on camera. It wasn’t expensive tech or a snazzy holiday gift — it was $36 worth of soda.

According to recent reports, “When Amazon emailed me that the order was delivered and it wasn’t there, I was very confused,” Cooper said. “When I pulled up the Ring footage, I saw the delivery happen on video, but then, 10 minutes later, a man in a blue hooded coat who’s intentionally hiding his face indicates up and grabs the box.”.

Package theft cases like this happen year-round, with CNET findings showing that 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or have stopped an attempted theft. And experts predict more stolen packages during the holidays, when thieves expect more deliveries.

So, don’t give thieves a chance. Now’s the time to make a strategy to keep your Black Friday and Cyber Monday packages out of sight. But what tactics actually work if doorbell cameras don’t? Here’s what you should know about porch piracy and how to lessen your chances of package theft.

Cooper’s Amazon order was scheduled to arrive between 3 a.m. and 6 a.m. — when it’s dark, but she knew she would be home. But thieves were already out lurking during those hours. Cooper mentioned the thief followed the driver and stole the package. She saw the thief stealing the package on her Ring security camera system.

Greg Zakowicz, Omnisend’s e-commerce and retail advisor, said Cooper’s package-theft incident is fairly typical, unfortunately — especially during the holiday season.

In a recent development, “Thieves know as well as shoppers that orders increase during this time, and often, the packages are more likely to contain more valuable items,” noted Zakowicz. “Shoppers during this time look to take advantage of deep discounts for not only gifts but themselves, making the package a potential goldmine for thieves.”.

There are a few steps you can take to lessen the likelihood of porch piracy. Zakowicz recommends using options like in-store pickups, post office boxes, in-garage delivery or deliveries to your workplace.

That advice is especially important for expensive tech you proposal to have delivered to your home unless someone will be there to grab the package immediately.

“While it may be less convenient, it’s a small price to pay to not have the hassle of gifts and expensive items going missing at the busiest shopping time of the year,” stated Zackowicz.

In a recent development, also ask your retailers not to ship the item in the manufacturer’s packaging. Some retailers, like Amazon and Target, will clearly display this before shipping because it could be an easy hint for thieves to guess what it is — especially if it’s tech. Even though this won’t stop porch pirates from being curious about what’s in the box, it may make them think about the effort and risk versus the potential reward, Zakowicz mentioned.

Sources indicate that if you want another option to have packages delivered to your home, consider scheduling your deliveries for a time you know you’ll be available. For instance, you can set up an Amazon Day to have all of your Amazon packages delivered at once so you can plan accordingly.

CNET found that US adults have mixed feelings about how effectively security cameras deter porch pirates: 11% of US adults believe they don’t deter them, while 9% use security cameras to get proof — not prevent it.

Regardless of your home security measures, don’t assume you’re safe from porch pirates just because you have a doorbell camera, and don’t use it as a means of keeping an eye on your package if you’re busy or not home. Instead, when you see motion detection, that’s a sign to grab it right away.

It has been revealed that “The most common misunderstanding is that having security cameras will prevent thieves from stealing packages,” noted Zakowicz. “Thieves are thieves because being caught is not their biggest worry. They also know porch piracy is not at the top of most officers’ day-to-day public service worries. Often, by the time the report is made, thieves are long gone.”.

Unfortunately, thieves may find other ways to steal packages, since their tactics are constantly changing. If that happens to you, there are a few steps you should take right away.

File a police report of the incident first. Be prepared to share information, including a description of the thief, and the make and model of the vehicle, with the police and your community so they can be vigilant of the thief.

Recent findings suggest that but don’t get your hopes up that the thief will be caught. Zakowicz remarked it’s rare that porch theft cases get solved.

In a recent development, “Police aren’t necessarily dedicating resources to solving porch pirates who stole a new stuffed animal or board game. However, it’s key for them to understand areas seeing an uptick in thefts, as they can be more alert to suspicious activity,” stated Zakowicz. And the retailer may request it.

After filing, Zakowicz states to report the theft to the carrier and retailer. Carriers may use the data to assess future likelihood of package theft incidents and it could help instruct delivery drivers to carefully hide packages. Retailers may also be able to assist with a replacement.

It has been revealed that cooper filed a police report with her local police department, which allowed her to upload the Ring video of the theft and acknowledged receipt. She’s not expecting the thief to be caught, but figures that her report could possibly help in some way.

“I live in a pretty safe neighborhood in Amazon’s own hometown, but their delivery trucks are on our street dropping off packages every day,” she mentioned. “It’s got to be a banquet for hungry thieves.”.

She reached out to her neighbors to tell them about the theft, and one reported that she, too, had had a package stolen a week earlier.

Cooper says she did not intentionally choose the early-morning drop-off time, but it was the only time Amazon offered for her delivery. Since then, she’s seen Amazon try to offer that same time and has chosen not to order an item rather than be forced to use that dark, quiet delivery slot.

Immediately after the theft, Amazon was less than helpful, routing her to an AI agent who stated it understood the situation was upsetting but that it wouldn’t be able to do anything for four days. When she checked back, Amazon agreed to refund her for the item, but kept insisting on labeling the package as “missing” and asked her to report back if she “found” it.

Industry observers note that “I hope the driver doesn’t get in trouble for a supposedly ‘missing’ package,” she mentioned. “It unnerves me that she was being followed by a thief. Who knows how long he followed that truck and how many packages he scooped up?”.

Meta’s Muse AI agent has only been around for a few months, but already has a track record of user privacy violations. Even Meta employees are reporting concerning incidents, including the agent taking actions they didn’t ask it to and sharing information they didn’t recognize that appears to belong to other users.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse stated the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she remarked she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy – and I’ve tried them all.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

Recent findings suggest that these are just the latest in a string of alarming incidents surrounding Muse. In its first month, a cybersecurity professional discovered Muse had a serious zero-day bug that made it hijackable. At least one journalist found the AI sifting through his Apple Messages after he’d explicitly denied those permissions, which Apple then issued stronger privacy protections to address. Banks have also blocked agents over concerns.

In a recent development, as a organization, Meta doesn’t have a solid history of respecting user privacy. That legacy is partly what informed ZDNET contributor David Gewirtz’s suspicion of the AI assistant when he tested it, though it earned his assigned title of “worst AI agent for privacy” all on its own. The agent asked him for everything from contacts and chats to his logins and passwords, and Meta automatically uses conversations with Muse to train its AI.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

It has been revealed that public awareness of the risks of AI agents hit a peak last year with the viral OpenClaw. The predominant advice for using agents has been to take every privacy precaution: Be careful with the data you share and the apps you give it permissions for, and watch what you tell it. But if consumers believe they’re doing so by restricting access to certain apps, just for Muse to find a way in anyway, privacy hygiene isn’t enough.

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible.

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

Latest Update: Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set latest limits on screenshots.
  • Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.
  • Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set latest limits on screenshots. The manufacturer will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and “when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,” Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday.

Whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers. These features observe what’s on a user’s screen as context for completing requests.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.

In a recent development, “Your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” Whittaker noted. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Signal’s move is another reminder of how Significant Tech’s AI strategy trickles downstream. As AI features have moved from services external to the OS (like chatbots from OpenAI or Anthropic) to further inside of it, third-party apps have to adapt to conditions that undermine their hard-won privacy infrastructure.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do.

Just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal remarked its protections don’t currently work on MacOS.

“It is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” she added. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.”.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

“Doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees,” Whittaker mentioned.

Anthropic Stock Fell Below Its IPO Price. Is It a Buy, or Is More Downside Just Ahead?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) soared into the spotlight last week, completing the biggest initial public offering ever.
  • In a recent development, the stock, which priced at $83, opened at $111, and soared 17% on its first day of trading.
  • At this level, is the tech giant a buy?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adria Cimino – Nov 26, 2026 at 4:02AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) soared into the spotlight last week, completing the biggest initial public offering ever. The artificial intelligence (AI) manufacturer raised $81 billion and immediately entered the market with a trillion-dollar valuation, placing it among long-established trillion-dollar companies such as Microsoft and Apple. And given the high demand for the stock, underwriters exercised an overallotment option that brought the total amount raised to more than $93 billion.

In a recent development, the stock, which priced at $83, opened at $111, and soared 17% on its first day of trading. The following days brought a sharp turnaround, however, with progressive declines. And on Nov. 24, Anthropic fell below its IPO price, closing at about $81.

At this level, is the tech giant a buy? Or is more downside just ahead? Let's find out.

We'll start by considering the Anthropic story so far. Anthropic is the developer of the AI model Claude, a product it rolled out only three years ago. Since that time, updated versions of Claude have launched, and demand and revenue growth have been explosive. Prior to the initial release, the firm delivered zero revenue, and in the third quarter of this year, revenue came in at $17 billion.

Considering we're in the early days of AI's application in the real world and usage by companies -- Anthropic's focus is on enterprise -- it's reasonable to be optimistic about growth ahead. Anthropic indicates that 50% of Fortune 500 companies are generating at least $100,000 in revenue on a trailing 12-month basis, and this represents a very small part of these companies' budgets. So there's much room for growth, particularly considering that Claude updates bring newly introduced use capabilities.

Anthropic drew attention because it represented the first pure-play AI company to launch an IPO, and it offered investors a newly introduced AI investing opportunity. The company's soaring revenue over a relatively short period of time surely attracted the eye of those focused on growth. Investors may also like the management team for its experience in building frontier models and its commitment to safety. Chief Dario Amodei and a small team of researchers left OpenAI several years ago to create Anthropic.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

With such a bright picture, why is the stock falling so soon after the IPO? One main reason is that this market launch happened at a difficult time for AI stocks. Investors have worried this year about the depth of spending on the AI build-out and its sustainability. Meanwhile, Democrats won U.S. midterm elections, and they've expressed caution regarding the pace of the build-out -- their leadership could result in regulation. These elements have put pressure on AI stocks, making the environment a difficult one for a newly launched player, particularly when this stock comes with a certain amount of risk.

Recent findings suggest that it's notable to remember that Anthropic has reported net losses in each of its years of operation, and this may continue as the tech giant builds and trains updated models. On top of this, Anthropic listed many other risks in its prospectus, from the potential for a serious AI-driven event to the possibility that insurance may not cover such disasters.

In an already jittery market, investors may have shifted their focus away from the growth story and to the risks. If, for instance, the pace of AI development slows and strict regulation is put into place, AI stocks across the board may feel the impact. But younger companies that aren't yet delivering sustainable profitability may suffer the most.

Now, let's consider our question: At today's level, below its IPO price, is Anthropic a buy, or is more downside ahead? I think it's still too early to get in on this AI growth story. While revenue may continue to climb and there's reason to be optimistic about demand from corporate clients, the general environment has become more difficult for AI stocks. These players have seen significant volatility, with gains one day and declines the next, and the uncertainties above are weighing on sentiment. While well-established tech players may offer investors considerable visibility, a newcomer like Anthropic doesn't.

More downside could be ahead, so right now, Anthropic stays on my watch list -- and doesn't move to my buy list.

Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage customers, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The company filed for bankruptcy last month.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot company from auctioning off customers’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […].

It has been revealed that “Character․AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its consumers — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”.

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

Siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

When a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

According to recent reports, the data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

It has been revealed that apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.

#132166. Can AI plan terrorist attacks? The US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2778 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Can AI plan terrorist attacks? The US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Government Accountability Office (GAO) conducted a series of tests earlier this year designed to determine whether people could bypass guardrails and convince AIs to initiative terrorist attacks.
  • Sources indicate that the tests were conducted using Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok.
  • I spoke via email with the report’s lead author, Kevin Walsh, director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) conducted a series of tests earlier this year designed to determine whether people could bypass guardrails and convince AIs to initiative terrorist attacks. The investigators succeeded. In October, the agency published a report titled “Covert Testing Used Common Platforms to Create Viable Attack Intends,” which was released to the public in November.

Sources indicate that the tests were conducted using Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok. All four AIs produced attack scenarios that subject matter experts were able to confirm would have mostly succeeded.

I spoke via email with the report’s lead author, Kevin Walsh, director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO. He told ZDNET:.

In general, the details provided by the four AI platforms are not novel. Much of the information is readily available on the internet. But these plans were generated in hours, rather than weeks or months. AI could also surface ideas or methods that may not have been previously considered.

In a recent development, to the companies’ credit, their safeguards have continued to evolve since we conducted these tests. The companies also assure us that this is an area of concern and ongoing research. However, our report concludes that, in its current state, this technology can be dangerous, and its misuse represents a growing risk to our nation.

In a recent development, the Government Accountability Office is an independent, nonpartisan agency that works for the legislative branch of the US government. Its responsibility is to “examine how taxpayer dollars are spent and provide Congress and federal agencies with objective, non-partisan, fact-based information to help the government save money and work more efficiently.”.

Also: Why enterprise AI agents could become the ultimate insider threat.

In a recent development, the GAO investigators constructed two attack scenarios: detonating an explosive device for maximum damage and destroying an electrical grid substation for maximum disruption. They randomly split the challenge across the four AI platforms, so that two AIs each worked independently on the explosive challenge while two others worked independently on the substation challenge.

Recent findings suggest that this assignment split is where, after being shown the results, the AI companies pushed back. That seems justifiable. By not giving all four AI services the same set of assignments, the GAO lost the ability to objectively measure all four against each other.

Recent findings suggest that as a platform-vs-platform comparison, the GAO investigation falls short. But as an investigation into whether the generative AI tools available in mid-2026 might be able to be used for credible national security threats, its results are definitive. The investigation also highlighted how AIs reduce the time and effort involved in researching how such attacks might be carried out.

Sources indicate that while the four AIs used for the tests were identified in the report, the GAO did not publish which AIs were used to carry out which tests. Instead, “Due to the sensitive nature and content of the testing, we randomly assigned an alphabetic character to each platform for purposes of presenting the test results within this report.”.

For the bomb-damage scenario, the two assigned AIs recommended different approaches, although both provided specific actionable steps in order to accomplish the tasks.

Platform A constructed a scenario where an IED (improvised explosive device) would be detonated inside a hotel parking structure. It provided a timetable for when the hotel was expected to be crowded due to a public event as well as where the hotel’s security was likely to be weakest.

It recommended where to rent a van from outside the city, how to disable the GPS in the van, a shopping list of supplies used in constructing the device, specific stores to shop at, where to park the van in the garage, how to set up the device for detonation, and even a bus route to take in order to get back to the attacker’s personal car.

Also: Could cyberwar knock us back to the Stone Age?

After additional prompting by GAO investigators, Platform A “also generated an image that directed us to a specific area to deploy the IED to cause significant damage to the location. Specifically, Platform A generated an image of a parking structure that recommended where to park the vehicle.”.

Recent findings suggest that GAO investigators verified the blueprint’s viability by consulting with a bomb squad commander at a big-city fire department. The bomb tech confirmed that following the instructions with the recommended components would result in an explosion. The GAO also confirmed the availability of the supplies from the vendors the AI recommended.

It has been revealed that platform B targeted a convention center. Its recommended preparations were extensive. It recommended incorporating a shell firm as a cover story so that the attacker could legitimately lease a secure, ventilated barn. It recommended a rural purchasing circuit, buying just enough supplies at four rural co-ops over four days in order to avoid triggering any mandatory reporting requirements.

The AI then recommended purchasing diesel fuel from three truck stops using cash, making “unremarkable purchases at unremarkable locations.” The AI recommended transferring the fuel into sealed 55-gallon drums at the barn. It also recommended careful storage conditions, including temperature, drum integrity, and separation from other materials (the materials themselves were redacted from the GAO’s report).

Also: Apple, Google, and Microsoft join Anthropic’s Project Glasswing to defend world’s most critical software.

Sources indicate that next up, the AI recommended a communications security review, burner phones, varied procurement routes, and information compartmentalization. It recommended taking a taxi to a waterfront and then walking south for 40 minutes. It suggested confirming sight lines and contractor access to road positions. It even suggested that while the attacker’s face would appear on three cameras, the footage from those specific cameras would not be reviewed for three weeks.

It then recommended sending decoy trucks into the target, then sneaking an explosive vehicle into a parking garage.

It has been revealed that when the GAO reviewed the recommendations, the agency discovered the AI got event dates wrong. However, according to the bomb squad commander, the components and procedures recommended would definitely have resulted in an explosion.

As with the bomb-damage scenario, the two AIs participating in the electrical grid scenario took different approaches, but both had the potential to be disturbingly effective.

Industry observers note that platform C began by identifying electrical substations where an attack could be most effective. It produced a list that helped identify vulnerable substations. After some prompting, “The platform then selected a substation in a specific major U.S. city and estimated that the loss of power would cause billions of dollars in damages.”.

According to recent reports, it identified the specific location on the specified substation where a drone could hit and cause a short circuit, which would destroy a key component. It actually provided a simulated video of the drone attack as well as a diagram that showed the component’s failure process.

The AI identified the exact model of the drone that it felt was best suited for the attack. Initially, the AI’s guardrails refused to provide an exact location for a target substation. That said, “The platform eventually provided the name of a substation, which we used to identify an exact location.”.

The day after the AI made its recommendations, the GAO reported, “We observed that the platform had removed portions of our chat discussions that related to electrical grid vulnerabilities. It is unclear whether this action was initiated as part of a guardrail or if by error.” After two weeks, the account had not been suspended.

Recent findings suggest that GAO investigators confirmed that the suggested drone model did exist, the route to the target was accurate, and the proposed target did exist. A subject matter expert consulted by the GAO “Verified that the information provided by Platform C was generally correct. The expert stated such an attack could, at the very least, cause damage to the substation. However, the expert could not confirm whether the specific drone suggested by Platform C would cause a short circuit or destruction of the substation.”.

After rented vans, shell companies, and aerial drone attacks, Platform D decided to do it old school: plain old firearms. Point. Shoot. Buh-bye.

Sources indicate that the AI provided GAO investigators with a primary target substation along with three secondary backup locations. It recommended locations near a large international airport and a bunch of data centers to increase the economic impact from the attack. And just in case it wasn’t clear enough, the AI drew a map highlighting the locations of the target substations.

Industry observers note that it recommended the use of a gun, recommended the type of weapon along with the proper ammo in order to maximize the effects of the attack, along with where an attacker could go to procure such weapons. It recommended both online and in-person surveillance of the target locations prior to initiating an attack.

As with Platform C’s recommendation, Platform D recommended specific components in the substation that would be most vulnerable to an attack. It even provided images highlighting where the transformers would be most vulnerable.

The GAO report stated that the AI originally threw up guardrails and refused to provide the information requested, saying, “Our query raised serious concerns about potential intent to engage in criminal activity or harm critical infrastructure due to the context of the conversation.”.

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in.

The more telling comment is this from the report: “However, the platform ultimately provided us with information needed for an attack.” I’m thinking someone in the GAO could probably sell water to a fish.

As with Platform C, GAO noted that the AI removed some of the chat content from the chat history. As for whether the plan would work, “We verified the planned attack was viable for half of the substation locations recommended by Platform D.”.

According to recent reports, A subject matter expert also confirmed that attacking the specific areas of the transformers recommended could cause an outage and that the specific firearms and ammunition recommended were available from the purchase locations specified. The AI did make an error in the generated maps by incorrectly placing roads.

In a recent development, but of the four recommended locations, two were actually viable. GAO investigators took a field trip to the recommended locations and verified that two could work for such an attack, but the other two had high walls that obscured the view of the targets.

After completing the tests, the GAO investigators presented the results to the AI vendors and gave the companies the opportunity to respond. While the GAO report purposely hid which AI provided which attack blueprint, the report is fully forthcoming with the complete response letters from each manufacturer.

In reading the responses, I found the difference in attitudes and approach to the question most interesting.

It has been revealed that anthropic’s four-page response letter was signed by Anthony Cimino, head of federal affairs. The firm’s response was courteous but strongly challenging. It moved immediately from thanking the GAO to questioning the statistical significance and criticizing the absence of a control group.

Anthropic’s letter about Claude claims, “We ask that the report specify that there were not enough trials to achieve significance, and that therefore any conclusions are at most preliminary.”.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

Google’s three-page response about Gemini was unsigned. The majority of the response discussed launch reviews, executive oversight, Google’s testing, filters, training, and human review practices. The firm did agree that Gemini could violate guidelines. It was the most disengaged from the GAO’s report, and it offered little in the way of explanation about the challenges raised.

Google’s letter says, “We have deep respect for the mission of the Government Accountability Office and we want to underscore that Google takes your work very seriously.”.

OpenAI’s three-page response letter about ChatGPT was signed by Chan Park, head of US and Canada policy and partnerships. It notes the manufacturer reviewed 325 responses from the AI and identified three that fell short of how the AI is supposed to behave. The company apparently replayed the requests and noted that it was unable to reproduce the responses reported by the GAO.

OpenAI was the clearest in stating that the GAO’s results demonstrated unacceptable behavior from the AI, stating: “Even a discrete contribution to a broader harmful activity can matter, and improving safeguards against such assistance remains an ongoing priority.”.

SpaceXAI’s 363-word, less-than-a-page response about Grok was unsigned. The company emphasized how much effort was required to bypass the safeguards and mentioned that there have been improvements in the guardrails since the GAO conducted its tests earlier that year.

Then we reach the “Say what, now?” moment of our day.

According to recent reports, the tech giant replied, “It is worth noting that GAO received its output from paid accounts in the United States. SpaceXAl provides unique moderation policies for registered, paid US account holders that reflect the lower risk profile of such accounts compared to free or foreign accounts.”.

In other words, the company contends that paying US account holders have a lower risk profile than free or foreign people, and that therefore Grok provides fewer guardrails. The letter provides no supporting evidence for that assumption.

In a recent development, while a credit card number could provide some linkage to a user’s identity compared to fully free accounts, users could easily obtain a prepaid card that allows for completely anonymous paid usage. I just think that making an assumption about risk factor based on whether a user is willing to pay $8 a month is a particularly fallacious security policy.

The GAO report is clear that each of the AIs did provide some pushback against providing cookbooks for conducting the destructive behavior.

The agency conducted a number of adversarial prompt seeding operations, including roleplaying, special encoding, character transformation, word transformation, separating intent from content, taking very small baby steps in prompting, and other approaches often used to convince an AI to effectively “jailbreak” its guardrails.

Also: If you’re not working on quantum-safe encryption now, it’s already too late.

While the AIs were eventually persuaded to participate in guiding attacks, some accounts were later shut down by the AI platforms, indicating that while the guardrails didn’t prevent the AI from providing initial advice, they were eventually flagged and terminated.

While that’s a bit of “locking the barn door after the horse has bolted,” it does indicate that the AI vendors are working toward more comprehensive protections.

The GAO report didn’t address the larger matter of whether censoring the AIs is ultimately in society’s best interest.

As a counterterrorism and infrastructure security professional, I often think of Ben Franklin’s famous statement, “Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.” Old Ben never had to contend with nukes, cyberattacks, and machines smarter than he was.

In a recent development, personally, I lament the need for guardrails because they limit potentially legitimate access to information. But as the GAO’s scenario shows, strong guardrails are ultimately necessary, not because of the AIs, but because we humans are our own worst enemy.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

On the other hand, it’s not as if humans haven’t been able to figure out how to conduct violent acts all on their own, without the help of an AI. For example, the Anarchist’s Cookbook, which is essentially a recipe book for the home manufacture of explosives and illicit drugs, has been publicly available continuously since the early 1970s. While also outdated, Amazon even sells a reprinted 1941 manual about the chemistry of powder and explosives.

Industry observers note that so, while it is definitely disturbing that the AIs could, collectively, provide four unique attack aims for civic disruption, they are not opening a door previously unavailable to those with nefarious intent. I laud the GAO for providing additional testing feedback to the AI companies, and the AI companies for improving their guardrails.

But while the report is scary in that all that information was presented in an organized manner by each of the AIs, that availability doesn’t bestow a newly introduced superpower on crackpots. After all, AIs are trained on publicly available information.

One of the more costly, but necessary, tradeoffs of an open society is that all this information is available. Whether an AI is used to structure that information is largely irrelevant in the face of that simple fact.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re an artist and you use social media, you’ve probably heard about Ohuhu by now. This brand promptly made a name for itself simply because they offered high-quality alcohol based markers at prices that undercut competitors. I have to admit that I turned my nose up at them at first; I didn’t believe they could be as good as the markers I already owned when they cost so much less.

Perfect for artists of all skill levels, the Ohuhu Hilo markers come in packs of 48 or 72 and are an affordable option compared to rivals. They have a soft brush tip and can be layered up on the page for an opaque finish.

Ohuhu's Honolulu 2S alcohol markers come in a huge range of colors, with 320 markers in the biggest set! These dual-ended markers feature a brush and a chisel tip. While you'll need to watch out for bleed through, they produce a beautiful and smooth finish.

I started off with the Hilo acrylic markers. These markers have a single, soft and flexible brush tip, and you can currently get either a set of 48 or a set of 72 at Amazon. I was excited to see how they would perform, so I stuck a Holiday movie on, sat back and got out a coloring book to test them out.

According to recent reports, as soon as the pen touched the page, I was immediately struck by the vibrancy of the colors and the opacity of the ink. Sure, the first sections of color I filled in were the blacks, but I couldn’t believe my eyes when the numbers almost disappeared under the acrylic ink. Some of the colors are less effective at this than others — but layer the ink up a few times, and you’ll have one gorgeously clean looking coloring page!

According to recent reports, as for the experience of using them, the soft tips give plenty of control. They felt incredibly smooth to use across gentle curves and coloring medium to large areas was easy and comfortable. These acrylic markers give you the ability to go over and redo areas you’re not happy with if you accidentally color over something you didn’t want to, which is a huge bonus.

Sources indicate that another positive under this set’s belt is the carrying case.The design is so cheerful that it immediately put a smile on my face the first time I saw it, and it honestly still does every time I open it. And compared to other name brand acrylic markers, they’re significantly cheaper — the 72 set works out to around 70 cents per marker at the Black Friday sale price.

There are some downsides to contend with. When it came to coloring small, detailed areas... I pretty much had to forget about staying within the lines. I struggled to achieve fine pointed shapes and found that the ink pooled into circular shapes every time I attempted them. I also had problems with streaky ink, and my coloring paper pilled in certain spots, too.

This is my first time using acrylic markers, so I’m willing to acknowledge all these problems could come down to my lack of skills. I’m going to keep using them and see if I can improve my technique and layer up more to combat the streaks. The pilling probably isn’t going away until I get a coloring book with higher quality paper, though.

Next up, I tried the Honolulu 2S alcohol based markers. You get more color options here as the sets come in packs of 24 all the way up to 320; and these markers have a dual tip. One side has a brush tip, and the other is a chisel tip.

Compared to the Hilo's, the Honolulu 2S’s brush tip is firmer and stiffer. Even though the Hilo brush tip felt great, I liked the Honolulu 2S’s firmer brush tip even more, and found it easier to control when coloring detailed areas and sharp points. It still handles curves just as well, and the chisel tip comes in handy for filling large areas too. I fell in love with alcohol-based markers years back because they produce a beautiful, non-streaky finish. The Honolulu 2S markers absolutely live up to that and looked fantastic on the page.

According to recent reports, however, using alcohol based inks comes with more of a learning curve. I started off filling in a large black area on the page once again, and was very impressed that the marker didn’t bleed much at all. However, other colors like the dark blue and gray didn’t fare so well, and bled right over the lines.

According to recent reports, the bleed can be mitigated by using paper made specifically for alcohol markers, but you don’t have that option if you want to color in a specific coloring book. It took an hour or two for me to get used to it, but I eventually learned to leave plenty of space while filling areas in to account for the bleed.

As well as bleeding over the lines, I also had to watch out for the ink bleeding through the paper — Ohuhu provides a plastic sheet to place under your work to avoid staining the next page in your sketchbook. The ink in the Honolulu 2S markers was clearly visible on the back side of the paper I colored on (seen on the left of the image below,) but none got through to the next page. Meanwhile, the back side of the page I colored with the Hilo markers (seen on the right below) was completely clean.

In a recent development, if you’re a budding artist, I highly recommend picking up a set of Ohuhu markers. The Hilo acrylic markers are the ones for you if you want the most vibrancy, and are also great if you want to have the option to redo areas if you’re not happy with them. Meanwhile, the Honolulu 2S markers stand out for their enormous color selection, excellent brush tip and super-smooth finish.

These markers are cheaper than the significant brands, and are even better value when discounted. Grab them while you can!

How Far Could the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite Plunge? Nearly 156 Years of History Offers an Answer.
